questions.question: A 6-year-old boy has had developmental delay since 18 months of age and recurrent 20-minute tonic-clonic seizures since age 2. He is now ataxic and drops objects. A complete blood count shows no anemia and a normal mean corpuscular volume. Serum and red blood cell folate are only slightly below the reference range, but cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate is nearly undetectable. Whole exome sequencing identifies a homozygous missense variant in FOLR1. Which mechanism best explains the disproportionately low cerebrospinal fluid value?

answers.A: Deficient dihydrofolate reductase activity within choroid plexus epithelium
answers.B: Failure of receptor-mediated folate endocytosis at the choroid plexus
answers.C: Impaired proton-coupled folate transport across the duodenal brush border
answers.D: Increased catabolism of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate within the subarachnoid space
answers.E: Reduced polyglutamation of folates by folylpolyglutamate synthase in neurons

explanations.A: Loss of dihydrofolate reductase would impair conversion of folic acid to tetrahydrofolate systemically and produce megaloblastic anemia, not an isolated cerebrospinal fluid deficit.
explanations.B: FOLR1 encodes folate receptor alpha, which concentrates 5-methyltetrahydrofolate from blood into cerebrospinal fluid by endocytosis at the choroid plexus, so its loss produces cerebral folate deficiency with near-normal systemic folate.
explanations.C: A proton-coupled folate transporter defect blocks intestinal absorption and would lower serum, red cell, and cerebrospinal fluid folate together with megaloblastic anemia.
explanations.D: There is no described accelerated cerebrospinal fluid folate catabolism syndrome; the pathology here is failed transport into the central nervous system compartment.
explanations.E: Folylpolyglutamate synthase adds glutamates to retain folates inside cells and does not govern movement of folate from blood into cerebrospinal fluid.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with homozygous FOLR1 loss-of-function variants has an unsteady gait, refractory seizures, and a cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate concentration of 1.4 nmol/L despite a normal diet and a normal complete blood count. His neurologist wants to restore central nervous system folate. Which therapy is most appropriate?

answers.A: Betaine, oral, at high dose
answers.B: Cyanocobalamin, intramuscular, weekly
answers.C: Folic acid, oral, at standard dose
answers.D: Leucovorin, intravenous then oral
answers.E: Pyridoxine, oral, at high dose

explanations.A: Betaine provides an alternate methyl donor for remethylation of homocysteine and is used in homocystinuria, not to refill a depleted cerebrospinal fluid folate pool.
explanations.B: Cobalamin injections treat pernicious anemia and other cobalamin absorption defects, but this child's cobalamin status and methylmalonic acid are unaffected.
explanations.C: Standard oral folic acid is poorly effective because it must be reduced and still depends on the defective receptor pathway to reach cerebrospinal fluid.
explanations.D: Leucovorin (N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate) is an already-reduced folate that reaches the central nervous system through the reduced folate carrier at high doses and restores cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine is the cofactor for cystathionine synthase and would not raise central nervous system folate concentrations.

questions.question: A 5-month-old girl has failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, recurrent pneumonias, and a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 112 fL. Serum folate is very low, serum cobalamin is normal, and there is no evidence of malabsorption of fat or protein. Genetic testing shows a defect in the carrier that moves folate across the duodenal brush border at acidic luminal pH. Which transporter is defective?

answers.A: Cubam receptor
answers.B: Folate receptor alpha
answers.C: Multidrug resistance-associated protein 1
answers.D: Proton-coupled folate transporter
answers.E: Reduced folate carrier

explanations.A: Cubam is the ileal receptor for the cobalamin–intrinsic factor complex; its loss causes cobalamin deficiency with elevated methylmalonic acid, not isolated folate malabsorption.
explanations.B: Folate receptor alpha mediates endocytic folate uptake, most importantly at the choroid plexus, and its loss produces cerebral folate deficiency with preserved systemic folate.
explanations.C: Multidrug resistance-associated proteins export folates and antifolates from cells rather than absorbing them from the gut lumen.
explanations.D: The proton-coupled folate transporter carries folate across the apical enterocyte membrane in the acidic proximal small intestine, so its loss produces hereditary folate malabsorption with megaloblastic anemia.
explanations.E: The reduced folate carrier delivers 5-methyltetrahydrofolate and methotrexate into peripheral cells at neutral pH and is not the principal intestinal absorptive route.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman takes a prenatal vitamin containing synthetic folic acid. In her enterocytes the vitamin is converted stepwise into a form that can accept a one-carbon unit from serine before being released into the portal circulation. Which enzyme catalyzes the two sequential reductions that make this carbon loading possible?

answers.A: Dihydrofolate reductase
answers.B: Folylpolyglutamate synthase
answers.C: Methionine synthase
answers.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase

explanations.A: Dihydrofolate reductase reduces folic acid to dihydrofolate and then dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, the only folate species able to accept a one-carbon unit.
explanations.B: Folylpolyglutamate synthase adds a glutamate tail that improves intracellular retention but performs no reduction of the pteridine ring.
explanations.C: Methionine synthase transfers the methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine and does not act on oxidized folates.
explanations.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase acts downstream, reducing N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate to N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate.
explanations.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase loads the carbon onto tetrahydrofolate but cannot generate tetrahydrofolate from folic acid.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with short bowel syndrome receives parenteral nutrition. His physician must ensure that the amino acid formulation supports one-carbon metabolism, because the major one-carbon unit loaded onto tetrahydrofolate in enterocytes and peripheral cells is transferred from a single amino acid, with glycine released as the by-product. Which amino acid is the principal one-carbon donor?

answers.A: Choline
answers.B: Formic acid
answers.C: Glycine
answers.D: Histidine
answers.E: Serine

explanations.A: Choline is a downstream product of S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation of phosphatidylethanolamine rather than the amino acid donating carbon to tetrahydrofolate.
explanations.B: Formic acid can be captured as N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, most notably during methanol detoxification, but it is not an amino acid and is not the routine donor.
explanations.C: Glycine is the product released when serine gives up its carbon, not the donor.
explanations.D: Histidine catabolism can contribute a formimino group to tetrahydrofolate but is a minor route compared with the serine reaction.
explanations.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase transfers the beta-carbon of serine to tetrahydrofolate to form N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate and glycine, the principal entry of carbon into the folate pool.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman planning pregnancy is found to be homozygous for a common methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase polymorphism. Enzyme studies show a thermolabile protein with a markedly increased KM for N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate but a nearly normal Vmax. Her physician recommends an increased daily folic acid intake before conception. Which explanation best accounts for the benefit of this recommendation?

answers.A: Elevated substrate concentration compensates for the variant enzyme's increased KM
answers.B: Folic acid directly stabilizes the thermolabile variant against proteolytic degradation
answers.C: Folic acid inhibits methionine synthase and thereby spares N5-methyltetrahydrofolate
answers.D: Higher intake removes the requirement for dihydrofolate reductase in the enterocyte
answers.E: Supplemental folic acid is converted to N5-methyl-THF without any need for MTHFR

explanations.A: An enzyme with an elevated KM approaches normal velocity only when substrate concentration is raised, so a larger folate pool restores N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate production.
explanations.B: Folic acid is a substrate precursor, not a chemical chaperone, and does not protect the variant protein from degradation.
explanations.C: Inhibiting methionine synthase would trap folate as N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate and worsen, not improve, one-carbon flow.
explanations.D: Dietary folic acid must still be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase regardless of the dose ingested.
explanations.E: There is no alternate enzyme that methylates tetrahydrofolate; methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase is the sole route to N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman at 31 weeks gestation reports 1 month of fatigue and exertional dyspnea. At 11 weeks she had viral gastroenteritis, and her appetite never returned. Serum cobalamin is normal and there is no evidence of marrow infiltration. Her studies are shown. Which statement best explains why a deficiency severe enough to cause pancytopenia developed over the course of a single pregnancy?

answers.A: Body folate stores of roughly 20 mg are exhausted within weeks of poor intake
answers.B: Folate is not stored at all and must be replenished several times each day
answers.C: Folate stores exceed 1.5 mg and are typically depleted only after several years
answers.D: Hepatic folate stores of about 200 mg are consumed over roughly two years
answers.E: Pregnancy triples maternal folate stores, which are then lost into the placenta

explanations.A: Total body folate is only about 20 mg, so reduced intake combined with the increased demand of pregnancy depletes stores in weeks to a few months.
explanations.B: Folate is stored, predominantly in red blood cells, which is why deficiency takes weeks rather than hours to appear.
explanations.C: Stores greater than 1.5 mg lasting years describes cobalamin, whose level is normal in this patient.
explanations.D: No folate store of that magnitude exists; overestimating the reserve would wrongly predict years of protection.
explanations.E: Pregnancy increases folate demand and lowers maternal stores rather than expanding them.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia initially responded to high-dose methotrexate, but his blasts now proliferate despite adequate plasma drug levels and normal drug delivery. Assays of the resistant blasts show normal dihydrofolate reductase amount and affinity and normal transporter-mediated drug influx, but methotrexate washes out of the cells within minutes. Which mechanism best explains the resistance?

answers.A: Amplification of thymidylate synthase that increases dTMP production
answers.B: Decreased folylpolyglutamate synthase activity that reduces drug retention
answers.C: Increased dihydrofolate reductase affinity for methotrexate over folate
answers.D: Increased proton-coupled folate transporter expression that raises influx
answers.E: Loss of serine hydroxymethyltransferase that blocks methylene-THF supply

explanations.A: Thymidylate synthase amplification would not cause the drug to leave cells rapidly and does not match the described washout kinetics.
explanations.B: Folylpolyglutamate synthase adds glutamate residues to both folates and methotrexate to trap them intracellularly, so reduced expression allows the drug to efflux and is a recognized resistance mechanism.
explanations.C: Higher affinity of dihydrofolate reductase for methotrexate would increase, not decrease, drug effect.
explanations.D: Increased transporter expression raises intracellular drug and would enhance sensitivity.
explanations.E: Loss of serine hydroxymethyltransferase would deplete one-carbon units and impair proliferation rather than confer resistance.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate followed 24 hours later by leucovorin. The pharmacist notes that leucovorin and methotrexate compete for entry into cells because they use the same carrier that normally delivers N5-methyltetrahydrofolate from plasma into peripheral tissues. Which carrier is being described?

answers.A: Cubam receptor
answers.B: Intrinsic factor
answers.C: Multidrug resistance protein 2
answers.D: Organic anion transporting polypeptide 1B1
answers.E: Reduced folate carrier

explanations.A: Cubam is the ileal endocytic receptor for the cobalamin–intrinsic factor complex and has no role in folate or antifolate uptake.
explanations.B: Intrinsic factor is a gastric parietal cell glycoprotein that binds cobalamin, not folates.
explanations.C: Multidrug resistance protein 2 is an efflux pump that removes drugs from cells rather than importing them.
explanations.D: Organic anion transporting polypeptide 1B1 mediates hepatic uptake of drugs such as statins and is not the folate route into peripheral cells.
explanations.E: The reduced folate carrier transports 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, leucovorin, and methotrexate into peripheral cells, which is why these agents compete for uptake.

questions.question: A 40-year-old healthy man volunteers for a nutrition study. Plasma is collected after an overnight fast and the folate species are separated chromatographically. Which folate species accounts for the great majority of circulating folate delivered from the enterocyte to peripheral tissues?

answers.A: Dihydrofolate
answers.B: Folic acid
answers.C: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate
answers.D: N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate
answers.E: N5-methyltetrahydrofolate

explanations.A: Dihydrofolate is a transient intracellular intermediate of dihydrofolate reductase and does not circulate in appreciable amounts.
explanations.B: Folic acid is the oxidized dietary and supplemental form; the enterocyte reduces and methylates it before export, so little unmetabolized folic acid circulates.
explanations.C: N10-formyltetrahydrofolate is an intracellular donor for purine ring carbons 2 and 8 rather than a plasma transport form.
explanations.D: N5,N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate is the intracellular substrate for thymidylate synthase and methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase.
explanations.E: Enterocytes reduce folic acid, load carbon from serine, and reduce it to N5-methyltetrahydrofolate, which is the dominant circulating folate, free or bound to albumin and folate receptor.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with new-onset confusion. He has eaten hospital meals and taken a multivitamin for 6 days before laboratory studies are drawn. His mean corpuscular volume is 104 fL and hypersegmented neutrophils are seen on smear. Which single test best reflects his folate status over the preceding 2 to 3 months rather than his recent intake?

answers.A: Homocysteine, serum
answers.B: Methylmalonic acid, serum
answers.C: Red blood cell folate
answers.D: Serum cobalamin
answers.E: Serum folate

explanations.A: Homocysteine rises in both folate and cobalamin deficiency and also responds quickly to repletion, so it is neither specific nor a long-term marker.
explanations.B: Methylmalonic acid is the gold-standard marker for cobalamin deficiency and is normal in isolated folate deficiency.
explanations.C: Red blood cells hold about 95% of body folate and are replaced over the erythrocyte lifespan, so red cell folate reflects folate status over months rather than days.
explanations.D: Serum cobalamin assesses a different vitamin and would not be corrected by folate repletion.
explanations.E: Serum folate fluctuates with recent dietary intake and can normalize within days of eating, masking chronic deficiency.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman in her first trimester eats no legumes, leafy greens, or citrus but consumes several servings of commercially produced bread, pasta, and breakfast cereal each day. Her physician notes that a federal program instituted in 1998 substantially reduced neural tube defects in the United States by adding folic acid to a specific food category. Which food category is fortified under this program?

answers.A: Butter and cream products
answers.B: Enriched breads, cereals, and pasta
answers.C: Fresh red meat and poultry
answers.D: Refined sugars and corn syrups
answers.E: Whole milk and other fluid dairy

explanations.A: Fats and dairy fats contain negligible folate and are not part of the fortification mandate.
explanations.B: Since 1998, enriched grain products in the United States must be fortified with folic acid, which is why this patient still receives meaningful folate despite avoiding legumes, greens, and citrus.
explanations.C: Meat is a good source of cobalamin rather than folate and is not fortified with folic acid.
explanations.D: Refined sugars contain no folate and are not vehicles for fortification.
explanations.E: Fluid milk is fortified with vitamin D, not folic acid.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman planning conception reports eating about 300 µg of naturally occurring food folate daily and taking a supplement containing 200 µg of folic acid with meals. Using the convention that 1 µg dietary folate equivalent equals 1 µg of food folate or 0.6 µg of supplemental folic acid taken with food, what is her approximate daily intake in dietary folate equivalents?

answers.A: 300 µg DFE
answers.B: 420 µg DFE
answers.C: 500 µg DFE
answers.D: 633 µg DFE
answers.E: 833 µg DFE

explanations.A: Counting only her food folate ignores the supplement entirely and understates her intake.
explanations.B: This figure would result from discounting rather than crediting the supplement's greater bioavailability.
explanations.C: Simply adding 300 and 200 treats supplemental folic acid as equivalent to food folate, which understates its absorption.
explanations.D: Because 0.6 µg of supplemental folic acid equals 1 µg DFE, her 200 µg supplement contributes about 333 µg DFE, which added to 300 µg from food gives roughly 633 µg DFE.
explanations.E: This value would require crediting the food folate itself with the supplement conversion factor, which double counts bioavailability.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman with osteosarcoma receives high-dose methotrexate and develops oral mucositis. She is given leucovorin, and her mucositis and cytopenias resolve while the antifolate is still measurable in plasma. Which property of leucovorin best explains the rescue?

answers.A: Bypasses dihydrofolate reductase because it is already a reduced folate
answers.B: Competitively displaces methotrexate from dihydrofolate reductase
answers.C: Enhances renal clearance of methotrexate and its polyglutamate forms
answers.D: Inhibits thymidylate synthase and thereby halts nucleotide consumption
answers.E: Is concentrated preferentially in tumor cells rather than in marrow cells

explanations.A: Leucovorin is N5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, an already-reduced folate that equilibrates with the one-carbon-loaded tetrahydrofolate pool without requiring the methotrexate-blocked dihydrofolate reductase step.
explanations.B: Leucovorin does not bind the enzyme active site in competition with methotrexate, which remains a tight-binding inhibitor.
explanations.C: Increased renal elimination is achieved with hydration, urinary alkalinization, or glucarpidase, not leucovorin.
explanations.D: Inhibiting thymidylate synthase would worsen, not relieve, the block on DNA synthesis.
explanations.E: Preferential tumor uptake would defeat the purpose of rescue, which is to protect normal proliferating tissue.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman asks her obstetrician whether the synthetic folic acid in her prenatal vitamin is chemically identical to the folate in the spinach she eats. The obstetrician explains that the term folic acid refers specifically to the most oxidized form of the vitamin. Which statement about the metabolic fate of this synthetic form is correct?

answers.A: Folic acid can donate a methyl group directly to homocysteine
answers.B: Folic acid is absorbed only after conjugation to a polyglutamate tail
answers.C: Folic acid must be reduced twice before it can carry a one-carbon unit
answers.D: Folic acid released from food is already the fully reduced folate species
answers.E: Folic acid requires cobalamin for its uptake into the enterocyte

explanations.A: Only N5-methyltetrahydrofolate acting through cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase can methylate homocysteine.
explanations.B: Polyglutamate tails are removed in the intestinal lumen before absorption and added back inside cells for retention.
explanations.C: Folic acid is the most oxidized folate and must be reduced by dihydrofolate reductase to dihydrofolate and then to tetrahydrofolate before it can accept a one-carbon group.
explanations.D: Food folates are a mixture of oxidation states, and the term folic acid denotes the oxidized species, not a reduced one.
explanations.E: Cobalamin is required for methionine synthase, not for intestinal folate uptake, which uses the proton-coupled folate transporter.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man eats a large serving of spinach, in which most folate exists as polyglutamate conjugates. Before this dietary folate can cross the enterocyte brush border, a specific luminal processing step must occur. Which step is required?

answers.A: Conjugation of additional glutamate residues by folylpolyglutamate synthase
answers.B: Methylation of the pteridine ring by methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.C: Oxidation of the folate and removal of the glutamate tail in the gut lumen
answers.D: Reduction to tetrahydrofolate by luminal dihydrofolate reductase
answers.E: Transfer of a one-carbon unit from serine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase

explanations.A: Polyglutamate addition occurs inside cells to improve folate retention and would further block, not enable, absorption.
explanations.B: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase acts on reduced folates inside cells and has no luminal role.
explanations.C: Dietary folates are oxidized and deconjugated in the intestinal lumen so that the monoglutamate form can be carried across the brush border by the proton-coupled folate transporter.
explanations.D: Reduction by dihydrofolate reductase occurs inside the enterocyte after absorption, not in the lumen.
explanations.E: Carbon loading from serine occurs intracellularly once tetrahydrofolate has been generated.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. The sulfonamide component blocks incorporation of para-aminobenzoic acid into the bacterial pteridine-containing vitamin. Her folate status remains normal throughout the course. Which statement best explains why her own one-carbon metabolism is spared?

answers.A: Human cells convert para-aminobenzoic acid to folate using dihydropteroate synthase
answers.B: Humans lack dihydropteroate synthase and absorb preformed folate from the diet
answers.C: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits human dihydrofolate reductase only at very high doses
answers.D: Trimethoprim is a potent inhibitor of the human proton-coupled folate transporter
answers.E: Trimethoprim spares human cells by inhibiting thymidylate synthase instead

explanations.A: Humans have no enzyme that condenses para-aminobenzoic acid with a pteridine group, which is precisely why the drug is selective.
explanations.B: Folate is a vitamin for humans because we cannot synthesize the pteridine–para-aminobenzoic acid–glutamate structure and must absorb it preformed, so blocking bacterial synthesis does not affect us.
explanations.C: Sulfamethoxazole targets bacterial folate synthesis and is not a meaningful inhibitor of human dihydrofolate reductase.
explanations.D: Trimethoprim acts on bacterial dihydrofolate reductase and does not block intestinal folate transport.
explanations.E: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, not thymidylate synthase, and its selectivity comes from far greater affinity for the bacterial enzyme.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl has developmental delay and seizures. Biochemical studies of cultured fibroblasts show accumulation of N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate with markedly reduced N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, while total cellular folate, serum cobalamin, and methylmalonic acid are all normal. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

answers.A: Dihydrofolate reductase
answers.B: Folylpolyglutamate synthase
answers.C: Methionine synthase
answers.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase

explanations.A: Dihydrofolate reductase deficiency would prevent formation of tetrahydrofolate itself, so no carbon-loaded folates would accumulate.
explanations.B: Loss of folylpolyglutamate synthase reduces total cellular folate retention rather than shifting the balance between two specific carbon-loaded forms.
explanations.C: Methionine synthase deficiency causes N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate to accumulate, the opposite of the observed pattern.
explanations.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase converts N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate to N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, so its loss causes the substrate to build up while the product falls.
explanations.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase deficiency would reduce the supply of N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate rather than cause it to accumulate.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man with psoriasis takes weekly low-dose methotrexate. His dermatologist explains that the drug binds the enzyme that regenerates the carbon-carrying folate species. Which change in the intracellular folate pool is the direct consequence of this enzyme blockade?

answers.A: Cobalamin becomes trapped, halting methionine synthase turnover
answers.B: Detoxification of formic acid by tetrahydrofolate is accelerated
answers.C: Dihydrofolate accumulates while tetrahydrofolate pools are depleted
answers.D: Folic acid accumulates because it can no longer enter the enterocyte
answers.E: N5-methyltetrahydrofolate accumulates and is exported into the serum

explanations.A: Cobalamin trapping is characteristic of nitrous oxide exposure, not of dihydrofolate reductase inhibition.
explanations.B: Formic acid clearance requires tetrahydrofolate, so a fall in tetrahydrofolate would slow rather than accelerate that reaction.
explanations.C: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, so dihydrofolate generated by the thymidylate synthase reaction cannot be recycled and builds up while tetrahydrofolate and its carbon-loaded derivatives fall.
explanations.D: Methotrexate does not block the proton-coupled folate transporter, and intestinal folic acid uptake continues.
explanations.E: Accumulation of N5-methyltetrahydrofolate describes the methyl trap of cobalamin deficiency, not antifolate therapy.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with untreated celiac disease has 6 months of diarrhea and weight loss. Duodenal biopsy shows severe villous atrophy of the proximal small intestine with a normal-appearing terminal ileum on imaging. Her studies are shown. Which explanation best accounts for the discrepancy between her two vitamin levels?

answers.A: Cobalamin absorption also requires the duodenum and should be equally impaired
answers.B: Cubam receptors are expressed in the duodenum rather than in the terminal ileum
answers.C: Folate is absorbed in the terminal ileum, which celiac disease characteristically spares
answers.D: Folate stores greatly exceed cobalamin stores, so folate necessarily falls first
answers.E: Proximal bowel absorbs folate via PCFT while ileal cobalamin uptake stays intact

explanations.A: Cobalamin is absorbed as the intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum, which is why her cobalamin and methylmalonic acid remain normal.
explanations.B: Cubam receptors are ileal; placing them in the duodenum would predict cobalamin deficiency, which she does not have.
explanations.C: Folate absorption occurs in the proximal small bowel through the proton-coupled folate transporter, not in the ileum.
explanations.D: Cobalamin stores exceed 1.5 mg and last years while folate stores are only about 20 mg, so the reasoning is reversed.
explanations.E: The proton-coupled folate transporter absorbs folate in the acidic proximal small intestine damaged by celiac disease, whereas cobalamin absorption occurs in the spared terminal ileum.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 3 hours after drinking an unlabeled solvent found in his garage. He is nauseated and complains that everything looks like a snowstorm. Arterial pH is 7.12 with a bicarbonate of 9 mEq/L. The toxicologist explains that the parent alcohol is itself relatively harmless and that toxicity requires its oxidation to an aldehyde and then to an acid. Which enzyme catalyzes the first of these two oxidations?

answers.A: Alcohol dehydrogenase
answers.B: Aldehyde dehydrogenase
answers.C: Catalase
answers.D: Cytochrome P450 2E1
answers.E: Formate dehydrogenase

explanations.A: Alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes methanol to formaldehyde, the committed first step that generates the toxic acid and is therefore the therapeutic target.
explanations.B: Aldehyde dehydrogenase catalyzes the second step, converting formaldehyde to formic acid, after the first oxidation has already occurred.
explanations.C: Catalase can oxidize ethanol in peroxisomes but is a minor pathway and not the principal route for methanol.
explanations.D: Cytochrome P450 2E1 contributes to ethanol metabolism at high concentrations and is not the main methanol-oxidizing enzyme.
explanations.E: There is no significant human formate dehydrogenase; formate is cleared through tetrahydrofolate-dependent oxidation to carbon dioxide.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man who drank a large amount of vodka is arousable with an arterial pH of 7.38 and a normal anion gap. His 38-year-old brother, who drank a solvent from the same garage in a comparable volume, has a pH of 6.9 and a bicarbonate of 3 mEq/L. Both alcohols are oxidized to their corresponding acids at similar rates. Which explanation best accounts for the acidosis in only one brother?

answers.A: Acetate is excreted unchanged by the kidney within minutes of formation
answers.B: Acetate is rapidly converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized, mostly in muscle
answers.C: Ethanol is oxidized far more slowly than methanol by alcohol dehydrogenase
answers.D: Formate is a weaker acid than acetate and therefore lowers the pH more
answers.E: Formate is produced only after tetrahydrofolate stores are fully exhausted

explanations.A: Acetate is not eliminated renally in significant amounts; it is metabolized, which is why it does not accumulate.
explanations.B: Acetate is quickly activated to acetyl-CoA and oxidized, largely in muscle, so it never accumulates, whereas formate is removed slowly by a tetrahydrofolate-dependent route and therefore builds up and acidifies the blood.
explanations.C: Ethanol is oxidized at least as fast as methanol, so differing rates of the first oxidation do not explain the difference.
explanations.D: Formate is not a weaker acid than acetate; the difference lies in the rate at which each is cleared.
explanations.E: Formate is generated as soon as methanol is oxidized and does not wait for folate depletion.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is found unresponsive with an arterial pH of 6.72, a bicarbonate of 4.8 mEq/L, and fixed dilated pupils. Blood ethanol, salicylate, and acetaminophen are undetectable, and lactate and ketones are far too low to explain the acidosis. The toxicology service immediately gives fomepizole while confirmatory levels are pending. Which action of this drug justifies its urgent administration?

answers.A: Alkalinizes plasma so that formate is trapped extracellularly
answers.B: Chelates circulating formate and promotes its renal elimination
answers.C: Inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, blocking formaldehyde and formate production
answers.D: Provides tetrahydrofolate so that formate is oxidized to carbon dioxide
answers.E: Saturates aldehyde dehydrogenase so that formaldehyde accumulates instead

explanations.A: Alkalinization is achieved with bicarbonate and is an adjunct that does not prevent further toxin formation.
explanations.B: Fomepizole does not bind formate; it prevents formate from being made in the first place.
explanations.C: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, halting conversion of methanol to formaldehyde and then formic acid, which is why it must be given before levels return.
explanations.D: Supplying folate to accelerate formate oxidation is the role of leucovorin or folic acid, not fomepizole.
explanations.E: Allowing formaldehyde to accumulate would increase toxicity, and fomepizole does not act on aldehyde dehydrogenase.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man arrives at a rural hospital 2 hours after ingesting windshield washer fluid. He is agitated, reports blurred vision, and has an arterial pH of 7.05 with a bicarbonate of 7 mEq/L. The pharmacy has no fomepizole in stock and the nearest supply is 4 hours away. Which intervention will most directly reduce further production of the toxic metabolite?

answers.A: Bicarbonate, which neutralizes the formic acid already formed
answers.B: Dialysis, which removes both methanol and formate from blood
answers.C: Disulfiram, which inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase activity
answers.D: Ethanol, which competes for the alcohol dehydrogenase active site
answers.E: Leucovorin, which speeds conversion of formate to carbon dioxide

explanations.A: Bicarbonate corrects the acidemia already present but does nothing to stop ongoing oxidation of methanol.
explanations.B: Dialysis removes toxin and is valuable in severe poisoning, but it does not act on the enzyme generating formate and is not immediately available in many settings.
explanations.C: Disulfiram blocks the second oxidation step and would cause aldehyde accumulation rather than prevent acid formation.
explanations.D: Ethanol is a competing substrate with much higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase, so it occupies the enzyme and slows conversion of methanol to formaldehyde and formate.
explanations.E: Leucovorin enhances clearance of formate that has already been produced rather than preventing its formation.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman with methanol intoxication has been started on fomepizole and sodium bicarbonate. Her serum formate remains elevated and she still cannot see hand motion. The team wants to accelerate the disposal of formate that has already been generated by supplying the cofactor that carries the formyl group to carbon dioxide. Which agent should be added?

answers.A: Activated charcoal
answers.B: Ethanol infusion
answers.C: Fomepizole
answers.D: Hemodialysis
answers.E: Leucovorin

explanations.A: Activated charcoal binds poorly to small alcohols and has no effect on formate already absorbed and metabolized.
explanations.B: Ethanol competes at alcohol dehydrogenase and is redundant in a patient already receiving fomepizole.
explanations.C: Fomepizole is already being given and prevents formate formation rather than removing existing formate.
explanations.D: Hemodialysis physically clears toxin but is a mechanical intervention, not the cofactor-based route the team is asking about.
explanations.E: Leucovorin supplies reduced folate so that formate is captured as N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate and then oxidized to carbon dioxide, regenerating tetrahydrofolate.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man recovers from a severe methanol ingestion after hemodialysis, but he remains unable to perceive light 2 weeks later. Pupillary responses are absent and funduscopy shows optic disc pallor. Which structures are the principal targets of formic acid in this patient?

answers.A: Both the retinae and the optic nerves
answers.B: Lateral geniculate nuclei bilaterally
answers.C: Occipital cortex, producing cortical blindness
answers.D: Oculomotor nerves, producing ophthalmoplegia
answers.E: Trochlear and abducens nerves bilaterally

explanations.A: Formic acid is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, which is why methanol poisoning classically produces blurred vision progressing to permanent blindness.
explanations.B: Thalamic relay nuclei are not the site of formate toxicity and would not produce optic disc pallor.
explanations.C: Cortical blindness spares pupillary responses and does not cause optic atrophy on funduscopy.
explanations.D: Oculomotor injury causes ptosis and gaze palsy rather than loss of light perception.
explanations.E: Trochlear and abducens palsies cause diplopia with intact vision, not blindness.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after drinking from a perfume bottle. He has vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, blurred vision, and agitation progressing to lethargy. Weight is 22 kg, blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 32/min, and heart rate is 148/min. Arterial blood gas shows pH 6.9, PaCO2 26 mm Hg, and bicarbonate 3 mEq/L. Which factor best explains his depressed level of consciousness?

answers.A: Ammonia accumulation from impaired urea cycle function
answers.B: Depression of the central nervous system by profound acidemia
answers.C: Formate-induced demyelination of the spinal dorsal columns
answers.D: Hypoglycemia caused by inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis
answers.E: Osmotic cerebral edema produced by a rising serum sodium

explanations.A: Hyperammonemia produces encephalopathy but is not a feature of methanol poisoning and would not generate this degree of anion gap acidosis.
explanations.B: Severe acidemia is itself a potent central nervous system depressant, and methanol produces neurologic depression comparable to ethanol on top of its formate-driven acidosis.
explanations.C: Dorsal column demyelination is the hallmark of cobalamin deficiency and develops over months, not hours.
explanations.D: Hypoglycemia can depress consciousness but is not characteristic of methanol ingestion and is not reflected in these gases.
explanations.E: Hypernatremic cerebral changes would require a markedly elevated sodium, which is not part of this presentation.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man is admitted 8 hours after drinking antifreeze. He has an anion gap metabolic acidosis, oliguria, and a rising creatinine, and his urine is shown below. Vision is normal. Which metabolite is the principal direct toxin to renal tubular cells and a major contributor to his anion gap?

answers.A: Formate
answers.B: Glycolaldehyde
answers.C: Glycolate
answers.D: Glyoxylate
answers.E: Oxalate

explanations.A: Formate is the toxic end product of methanol, and this patient has renal rather than ocular injury.
explanations.B: Glycolaldehyde is a transient intermediate formed by alcohol dehydrogenase and is rapidly oxidized further.
explanations.C: Glycolate is the metabolite that directly injures renal tubular cells and accounts for most of the anion gap in ethylene glycol poisoning.
explanations.D: Glyoxylate contributes to the acidosis but is short-lived and is largely converted onward to oxalate.
explanations.E: Oxalate causes injury indirectly by binding calcium and precipitating as crystals that obstruct tubules rather than by direct cellular toxicity.

questions.question: Two patients present the same evening with severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and altered mental status. The first, a 46-year-old woman, has fixed dilated pupils and cannot perceive light; the second, a 51-year-old man, has oliguria with calcium oxalate crystalluria and normal vision. Both are given fomepizole. Which statement best describes the difference in end-organ toxicity between the two ingestions?

answers.A: Both toxins damage the retina, but only methanol damages the kidney
answers.B: Ethylene glycol causes blindness while methanol causes renal failure
answers.C: Ethylene glycol produces neither acidosis nor organ-specific damage
answers.D: Methanol damages the eye while ethylene glycol damages the kidney
answers.E: Neither toxin produces a high anion gap metabolic acidosis

explanations.A: Ethylene glycol does not injure the retina, and methanol is not a renal toxin.
explanations.B: This reverses the classic pattern; blurred vision points to methanol and crystalluria points to ethylene glycol.
explanations.C: Ethylene glycol reliably produces a severe anion gap acidosis through glycolate, glyoxylate, and oxalate.
explanations.D: Formate from methanol injures the retina and optic nerve, whereas glycolate and oxalate from ethylene glycol injure renal tubules, while both produce severe acidosis treated with fomepizole or ethanol.
explanations.E: Both ingestions are defined clinically by a profound high anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is brought in obtunded with an arterial pH of 6.95 and a bicarbonate of 5 mEq/L. Lactate is 2.1 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.3 mmol/L, and salicylate is undetectable. The laboratory reports that serum methanol and ethylene glycol assays are sent to a reference laboratory with a 12-hour turnaround. Which principle should guide management now?

answers.A: Await the serum methanol and ethylene glycol levels before any therapy
answers.B: Bicarbonate below 8 mEq/L essentially excludes a toxic alcohol ingestion
answers.C: Normal lactate and ketone levels rule out toxic alcohol poisoning
answers.D: Serum osmolality provides no useful information in this situation
answers.E: Treat empirically when severe acidosis is otherwise unexplained

explanations.A: Confirmatory levels take longer than the treating physician can afford to wait, and delay allows more toxic metabolite to form.
explanations.B: A bicarbonate below 8 mEq/L is one of the findings that raises rather than lowers suspicion for a toxic alcohol.
explanations.C: Normal lactate and ketones are exactly what make the unexplained acidosis suspicious for methanol or ethylene glycol.
explanations.D: An elevated osmolal gap is a useful early clue supporting the presence of an unmeasured small alcohol.
explanations.E: Profound acidosis with a bicarbonate below 8 mEq/L that lactate, ketones, and salicylate cannot explain warrants immediate empiric alcohol dehydrogenase blockade.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his wife found him vomiting and stumbling in the garage. He takes metformin, dapagliflozin, and simvastatin, and was recently started on isoniazid after a positive tuberculin test. His speech is slurred and pupillary reflexes are decreased. Urinalysis shows no glucose, ketones, cells, casts, or crystals. Which finding in his studies best supports a toxic alcohol ingestion?

answers.A: An anion gap of 28 mEq/L with an osmolal gap of about 28 mOsm/kg
answers.B: An elevated lactic acid concentration that fully explains the acidosis
answers.C: Ketonuria accompanied by a markedly elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate
answers.D: Normal arterial pH with a fully compensated respiratory alkalosis
answers.E: Urinary calcium oxalate crystals together with acute kidney injury

explanations.A: The anion gap is 140 − 100 − 12 = 28 mEq/L and calculated osmolality is about 292 mOsm/kg, leaving an osmolal gap near 28, the combination that signals an unmeasured small alcohol.
explanations.B: His lactic acid is within the reference range and cannot account for a bicarbonate of 12 mEq/L.
explanations.C: Urinalysis shows no ketones, so a ketoacidosis is not the explanation despite his diabetes.
explanations.D: His pH is 7.30 with a low bicarbonate, which is an uncompensated metabolic acidosis, not a respiratory alkalosis.
explanations.E: The urine contains no crystals, which argues against ethylene glycol and in favor of methanol.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl is brought in 5 hours after being found next to an open bottle of cologne. She has vomited repeatedly, complains that she cannot see clearly, and is now drowsy. Her studies are shown, and a urine microscopy is unremarkable. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

answers.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
answers.B: Methanol intoxication
answers.C: Organophosphate poisoning
answers.D: Salicylate poisoning
answers.E: Sepsis with lactic acidosis

explanations.A: Her glucose is normal and serum ketones are negative, excluding ketoacidosis as the cause of this gap.
explanations.B: Visual blurring with a profound high anion gap acidosis unexplained by lactate or ketones after ingesting a cologne, which commonly contains methanol, identifies methanol poisoning.
explanations.C: Organophosphates cause miosis, bronchorrhea, and fasciculations without a formate-driven acidosis or visual blurring.
explanations.D: Salicylate poisoning typically causes tinnitus with a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis rather than isolated visual loss.
explanations.E: Her lactate is normal, which excludes sepsis-related lactic acidosis as the source of the gap.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman with confirmed methanol ingestion has received fomepizole 30 minutes ago. She is intubated, her arterial pH is 6.90, and her bicarbonate is 4 mEq/L. Her blood pressure is falling despite fluid resuscitation and vasopressors. Which additional therapy most directly addresses the acidemia while the toxin is cleared?

answers.A: Acetazolamide, intravenous
answers.B: Ammonium chloride, intravenous
answers.C: Bicarbonate, intravenous sodium
answers.D: Insulin with dextrose, intravenous
answers.E: Normal saline with potassium, intravenous

explanations.A: Acetazolamide causes bicarbonate wasting and would deepen the metabolic acidosis.
explanations.B: Ammonium chloride is an acidifying agent and is contraindicated here.
explanations.C: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate neutralizes formic acid and raises pH, supporting hemodynamics while alcohol dehydrogenase blockade and clearance take effect.
explanations.D: Insulin and dextrose treat hyperkalemia or ketoacidosis, neither of which is driving this acidosis.
explanations.E: Saline with potassium provides volume and electrolytes but does not correct a bicarbonate of 4 mEq/L.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman with a measured methanol concentration of 237 mg/dL has received fomepizole, intravenous folate, and repeated doses of sodium bicarbonate, yet her arterial pH remains 6.85 and she is comatose with fixed pupils. Which intervention is most appropriate next?

answers.A: Activated charcoal via nasogastric tube
answers.B: Ethanol infusion in addition to fomepizole
answers.C: Forced diuresis with intravenous furosemide
answers.D: Hemodialysis
answers.E: Repeat dosing of leucovorin every hour

explanations.A: Charcoal does not adsorb small alcohols and is useless hours after ingestion.
explanations.B: Adding ethanol to fomepizole provides no further enzyme blockade and adds central nervous system depression.
explanations.C: Forced diuresis does not appreciably clear methanol or formate and risks volume and electrolyte derangement.
explanations.D: Hemodialysis rapidly removes both methanol and formate and corrects acidosis, and is indicated for severe intoxication with refractory acidemia or visual loss.
explanations.E: Additional folate marginally accelerates formate oxidation but cannot correct a pH of 6.85 in a patient with this toxin burden.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man walks into the emergency department 30 minutes after intentionally swallowing about 100 mL of a solvent labeled as containing methanol. He is fully alert, protecting his airway, and has normal vital signs with an arterial pH of 7.40 and no visual complaints. Which management approach is most appropriate at this time?

answers.A: Administer activated charcoal after a 6-hour observation period
answers.B: Begin hemodialysis immediately regardless of his pH
answers.C: Delay all therapy until the serum methanol level returns
answers.D: Give naloxone and observe for return of consciousness
answers.E: Induce emesis and start an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor

explanations.A: Charcoal binds methanol poorly, and waiting 6 hours allows substantial conversion to formate.
explanations.B: Dialysis is reserved for severe intoxication with acidosis, visual symptoms, or very high levels, none of which he has yet.
explanations.C: Waiting for a level guarantees that toxic metabolite accumulates before treatment begins.
explanations.D: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity and has no role in alcohol ingestion in an alert patient.
explanations.E: In a conscious patient who has ingested methanol very recently, emesis can remove unabsorbed toxin, and blocking alcohol dehydrogenase prevents formate formation before acidosis or visual injury develops.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with methanol poisoning has a serum methanol concentration of 74 mmol/L. His physician notes that intracellular tetrahydrofolate is normally present at concentrations below 1 micromolar. Which conclusion about formate handling in this patient is most accurate?

answers.A: Cellular tetrahydrofolate is vastly outnumbered by the formate generated
answers.B: Formate cannot cross cell membranes to reach tetrahydrofolate at all
answers.C: Formate inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and thereby blocks its own supply
answers.D: N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate is a dead end that cannot be oxidized further
answers.E: Tetrahydrofolate is consumed stoichiometrically and is never regenerated

explanations.A: Formate produced from a millimolar methanol burden overwhelms a micromolar tetrahydrofolate pool, so the detoxification route saturates and formate accumulates until folate is supplied or the toxin is dialyzed.
explanations.B: Formate readily reaches intracellular folate; the limitation is cofactor abundance, not membrane access.
explanations.C: Formate does not inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase, and methanol continues to be oxidized unless the enzyme is blocked pharmacologically.
explanations.D: N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate is oxidized to carbon dioxide with regeneration of tetrahydrofolate, which is the basis of leucovorin therapy.
explanations.E: Tetrahydrofolate is regenerated after the formyl group is released as carbon dioxide, so it acts catalytically rather than stoichiometrically.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man who drank radiator antifreeze develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm 12 hours after ingestion. His creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.6 mg/dL and urine microscopy shows abundant envelope-shaped crystals. Which process best explains the combination of findings?

answers.A: Anion gap closure as oxalate is filtered and excreted
answers.B: Calcium oxalate precipitation causing hypocalcemia and tubular obstruction
answers.C: Hemolysis from oxidative injury to circulating red blood cells
answers.D: Optic disc edema progressing to irreversible loss of vision
answers.E: Rhabdomyolysis from direct toxic injury to skeletal muscle

explanations.A: Oxalate excretion does not close the anion gap, and gap closure would not cause tetany.
explanations.B: Glyoxylate is oxidized to oxalate, which binds ionized calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that lower serum calcium and obstruct renal tubules, producing tetany with acute kidney injury.
explanations.C: Ethylene glycol does not cause oxidative hemolysis, and the crystals point to oxalate rather than red cell destruction.
explanations.D: Ocular injury is the signature of methanol, and this patient's vision is unaffected.
explanations.E: Rhabdomyolysis would produce myoglobinuric pigment casts rather than envelope-shaped oxalate crystals.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man required dialysis after an ethylene glycol ingestion, and a 47-year-old woman in the adjacent bed lost all light perception after a methanol ingestion. Both were treated with fomepizole and both survived. Their families ask about long-term outcome. Which statement best describes the expected recovery?

answers.A: Both the visual loss and the renal injury are permanent
answers.B: Both the visual loss and the renal injury will fully recover
answers.C: Renal function usually recovers over days to months; vision does not
answers.D: Renal injury is permanent while vision typically recovers in weeks
answers.E: Visual loss recovers only if leucovorin is given within 24 hours

explanations.A: Kidney injury from ethylene glycol is generally reversible, so labeling both outcomes permanent is incorrect.
explanations.B: Formate-induced retinal and optic nerve damage is essentially irreversible, so full visual recovery should not be promised.
explanations.C: Ethylene glycol nephrotoxicity typically resolves over days to months as tubules regenerate, whereas methanol-induced retinal and optic nerve injury is essentially permanent.
explanations.D: This reverses the actual prognosis for the two organs involved.
explanations.E: Leucovorin accelerates formate clearance but does not restore vision once the retina and optic nerve are damaged.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder is found unresponsive with agonal breathing. Her family reports she said everything looked blurry shortly before collapsing. Arterial pH is 6.72 with bicarbonate 4.8 mEq/L and an anion gap of 29 mEq/L. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is 0.28 mmol/L, blood ethanol is undetectable, salicylate and acetaminophen are negative, and urine microscopy shows no crystals. Which ingestion best explains her presentation?

answers.A: Aspirin
answers.B: Ethanol
answers.C: Ethylene glycol
answers.D: Methanol
answers.E: Propylene glycol

explanations.A: Salicylate is undetectable, and aspirin toxicity usually produces a mixed respiratory alkalosis with tinnitus rather than blindness.
explanations.B: Blood ethanol is negative, and ethanol alone does not produce a severe anion gap acidosis because acetate is rapidly oxidized.
explanations.C: Ethylene glycol injures the kidneys and produces oxalate crystalluria, neither of which is present, and it does not cause visual loss.
explanations.D: Blurred vision with fixed pupils and a profound unexplained anion gap acidosis is the classic presentation of methanol poisoning with formate-driven retinal and optic nerve injury.
explanations.E: Propylene glycol toxicity typically follows prolonged infusion of certain drugs and causes lactic acidosis without visual loss.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman recovers after hemodialysis for a severe unexplained anion gap acidosis accompanied by transient blurred vision and fixed pupils. Her renal function and urine sediment remained normal throughout. On extubation she admits to drinking a household product as a substitute for liquor. Which product is she most likely to have consumed?

answers.A: Aftershave containing only ethanol and water
answers.B: Antifreeze poured from a radiator container
answers.C: Isopropyl alcohol rubbing solution
answers.D: Rubbing alcohol used to clean a wound
answers.E: Windshield washer fluid used as an ethanol substitute

explanations.A: Pure ethanol products cause intoxication without a severe anion gap acidosis because acetate is rapidly oxidized.
explanations.B: Antifreeze contains ethylene glycol, which injures the kidneys and produces oxalate crystalluria rather than visual loss.
explanations.C: Isopropyl alcohol produces ketosis without a large anion gap acidosis and does not damage the retina.
explanations.D: Rubbing alcohol is isopropyl alcohol, which causes an osmolal gap with ketonemia but not formate acidosis or blindness.
explanations.E: Windshield washer fluid is largely methanol, and its oxidation to formate explains both the profound acidosis and the ocular toxicity with normal kidneys.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man participating in a metabolic study is fed a defined formula while isotopically labeled substrates are traced into S-adenosylmethionine. The investigators explain that the activated methyl group cycle has exactly two kinds of carbon input. Which pair correctly identifies these inputs?

answers.A: Dietary methionine and the methyl group of N5-methyltetrahydrofolate
answers.B: Formate from methanol and the formyl group of N10-formyl-THF
answers.C: Homocysteine absorbed from the gut and adenosine from nucleotides
answers.D: Propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids and dietary cobalamin
answers.E: Serine from the diet and the methylene group of methylene-THF

explanations.A: The cycle is fed by methionine from the diet or intracellular protein turnover and by methyl groups delivered from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate through cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase.
explanations.B: Formate enters the folate pool as N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate and is used for purine carbons or oxidized to carbon dioxide, not fed into the methyl cycle.
explanations.C: Homocysteine is generated within the cycle rather than absorbed, and adenosine is a product of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolysis, not an input.
explanations.D: Propionyl-CoA enters the citric acid cycle through methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a separate cobalamin-dependent reaction.
explanations.E: Serine donates carbon to tetrahydrofolate to form methylene-THF, which must first be reduced by MTHFR before that carbon can enter the methyl cycle.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with a rare inborn error is studied to define where carbon and sulfur leave the activated methyl group cycle. Her physician explains that the cycle has two kinds of output. Which pair correctly describes them?

answers.A: Adenosine donated to purine salvage and glycine to heme synthesis
answers.B: Methyl groups donated by SAM and homocysteine entering transsulfuration
answers.C: Propionyl-CoA entering the citric acid cycle and free methionine
answers.D: Succinyl-CoA for heme synthesis and cysteine used only for glutathione
answers.E: Tetrahydrofolate for purine synthesis and formate oxidized to carbon dioxide

explanations.A: Adenosine is released when S-adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolyzed but is not a functional output of the cycle, and glycine comes from the folate reaction with serine.
explanations.B: S-adenosylmethionine donates methyl groups to a wide range of acceptors, and homocysteine that is not remethylated leaves the cycle through transsulfuration toward cystathionine and cysteine.
explanations.C: Propionyl-CoA metabolism is a distinct cobalamin-dependent pathway unrelated to the outputs of the methyl cycle.
explanations.D: Succinyl-CoA arises from methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and cysteine derived from transsulfuration serves many purposes beyond glutathione.
explanations.E: These are folate pool reactions rather than outputs of the activated methyl group cycle.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man has 4 months of paresthesias, an unsteady gait, and forgetfulness. Examination shows absent vibration sense in the feet and hyperreflexia. His laboratory studies are shown. The reaction that links the folate pool to the activated methyl group cycle is failing in this patient. Which enzyme catalyzes that reaction using methylcobalamin?

answers.A: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase
answers.B: Cystathionine synthase
answers.C: Methionine synthase
answers.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.E: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

explanations.A: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase remethylates homocysteine using betaine and requires no cobalamin, which is why betaine can be used therapeutically.
explanations.B: Cystathionine synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate to move homocysteine out of the cycle rather than to transfer a folate methyl group into it.
explanations.C: Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to transfer the methyl group from N5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, the single reaction connecting the folate pool to the activated methyl group cycle.
explanations.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase generates N5-methyltetrahydrofolate but uses flavin, not cobalamin.
explanations.E: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses deoxyadenosylcobalamin and explains this patient's elevated methylmalonic acid, but it is not part of the methyl cycle.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with chronic liver disease has reduced hepatic capacity to generate the universal methyl donor despite adequate dietary methionine. Her hepatologist explains that formation of this donor is unusual because it consumes a high-energy cofactor in a way that yields no nucleoside diphosphate. Which reaction generates S-adenosylmethionine?

answers.A: Acetyl-CoA is condensed with methionine to form a thioester
answers.B: Betaine donates a methyl group directly to methionine
answers.C: Cobalamin is adenosylated using GTP as the adenosyl donor
answers.D: Methionine is condensed with ATP, releasing all three phosphates
answers.E: Serine is decarboxylated and then joined to adenosine

explanations.A: Methionine is not activated as a thioester; the sulfur atom is instead alkylated by an adenosyl group.
explanations.B: Betaine donates a methyl group to homocysteine to regenerate methionine, a step upstream of adenosylation.
explanations.C: Adenosylation of cobalamin produces the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and is a separate reaction.
explanations.D: Methionine adenosyltransferase attacks ATP so that the entire adenosyl group is transferred to the methionine sulfur, releasing phosphate and pyrophosphate and creating the reactive sulfonium ion.
explanations.E: Serine contributes carbon to the folate pool and to phospholipid head groups but is not the precursor of S-adenosylmethionine.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has developmental delay, myopathy, and markedly elevated plasma methionine with elevated S-adenosylhomocysteine but only mildly increased homocysteine. His plasma total homocysteine fails to rise appropriately when methionine is loaded. Which enzyme deficiency best explains the accumulation of the demethylated adenosyl intermediate?

answers.A: Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase
answers.B: Cystathionine gamma-lyase
answers.C: Methionine adenosyltransferase
answers.D: Methionine synthase
answers.E: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase

explanations.A: Loss of betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase would raise homocysteine rather than cause the adenosyl intermediate to accumulate.
explanations.B: Cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency causes cystathionine to accumulate downstream of homocysteine.
explanations.C: Methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency raises methionine but lowers rather than raises S-adenosylhomocysteine.
explanations.D: Methionine synthase deficiency elevates homocysteine and lowers methionine, the opposite of this pattern.
explanations.E: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase releases homocysteine and adenosine after SAM donates its methyl group, so its loss causes S-adenosylhomocysteine to accumulate without producing homocystinuria.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man is placed on a strictly methionine-restricted diet for a metabolic disorder. His physician warns that the single largest consumer of methyl groups in the body will be affected first, because the product of that pathway is continuously lost in urine as an anhydride and must be resynthesized daily. Which pathway consumes the most S-adenosylmethionine?

answers.A: Creatine synthesis to replace creatinine lost in the urine
answers.B: DNA methylation at cytosine residues by DNA methyltransferases
answers.C: Epinephrine synthesis from norepinephrine in the adrenal medulla
answers.D: Histone lysine methylation for epigenetic gene regulation
answers.E: Phosphatidylcholine synthesis for cell membranes and myelin

explanations.A: Creatine synthesis is the largest metabolic use of S-adenosylmethionine because phosphocreatine is continuously lost as creatinine in urine and must be replaced.
explanations.B: DNA methylation is biologically critical but consumes a small fraction of the total methyl flux.
explanations.C: Epinephrine synthesis uses a very small quantity of methyl groups relative to creatine turnover.
explanations.D: Histone methylation is regulatory and involves comparatively minute amounts of substrate.
explanations.E: Phospholipid methylation is a major use but still less than creatine synthesis.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl with a guanidinoacetate methyltransferase defect has intractable seizures and developmental delay, and brain magnetic resonance spectroscopy shows an absent creatine peak. Her neurologist explains why loss of this S-adenosylmethionine-dependent product is so damaging to neurons. Which statement best describes the normal role of the missing compound?

answers.A: Creatine directly reduces NAD+ to NADH within the cytosol
answers.B: Creatine transports ADP across the inner mitochondrial membrane
answers.C: Creatinine is reconverted to creatine in the kidney for reuse
answers.D: Phosphocreatine shuttles high-energy phosphate away from mitochondria
answers.E: Phosphocreatine substitutes for oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor

explanations.A: Creatine takes no part in redox chemistry and does not reduce nicotinamide cofactors.
explanations.B: ADP is carried across the inner membrane by the adenine nucleotide translocase, not by creatine.
explanations.C: Creatinine is a dead-end product excreted in the urine and cannot be salvaged.
explanations.D: Creatine kinase transfers phosphate between ATP and creatine at the mitochondrion and again at distant sites, so the creatine–phosphocreatine pair effectively shuttles high-energy phosphate and helps ADP return to mitochondria, supporting energy balance in the central nervous system.
explanations.E: Phosphocreatine is a phosphate reservoir and has no role in terminal electron transfer.

questions.question: A 4-month-old infant with a severe defect in the activated methyl group cycle has delayed myelination on magnetic resonance imaging. Biochemical analysis shows depletion of a class of S-adenosylmethionine-derived membrane lipids that possess antioxidant properties and are abundant in myelin. Which products are most likely depleted?

answers.A: Carnitine and its short-chain acyl esters
answers.B: Creatine and phosphocreatine in muscle
answers.C: Phosphatidylcholine and plasmenylcholine
answers.D: Sphingomyelin generated from ceramide and serine
answers.E: Taurine-conjugated bile salts secreted in bile

explanations.A: Carnitine is derived from trimethyllysine released during protein degradation and is a fatty acid carrier, not a myelin membrane lipid.
explanations.B: Creatine supports energy buffering rather than forming the myelin membrane itself.
explanations.C: S-adenosylmethionine methylates phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine and supports plasmenylcholine, a plasmalogen with antioxidant properties that is a major constituent of myelin and plasma membranes.
explanations.D: Sphingomyelin synthesis draws its head group from existing phosphatidylcholine and is not itself a direct SAM methylation product.
explanations.E: Bile salt conjugation with taurine is unrelated to S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation of membrane lipids.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman undergoes resection of an adrenal medullary tumor that secretes large amounts of epinephrine. The pathologist notes that this tumor expresses the enzyme catalyzing the final S-adenosylmethionine-dependent step of catecholamine synthesis, a step largely restricted to the adrenal medulla. Which enzyme is being described?

answers.A: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase acting on DOPA
answers.B: Catechol-O-methyltransferase acting on epinephrine
answers.C: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase acting on dopamine
answers.D: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase acting on norepinephrine
answers.E: Tyrosine hydroxylase acting on tyrosine

explanations.A: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase uses pyridoxal phosphate to convert DOPA to dopamine and consumes no methyl groups.
explanations.B: Catechol-O-methyltransferase does use S-adenosylmethionine, but it degrades catecholamines rather than synthesizing epinephrine.
explanations.C: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase is a copper- and ascorbate-dependent hydroxylase that makes norepinephrine.
explanations.D: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to norepinephrine to form epinephrine, largely in the adrenal medulla.
explanations.E: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting hydroxylation using tetrahydrobiopterin and involves no methylation.

questions.question: A researcher studying genomic imprinting and X-chromosome inactivation depletes S-adenosylmethionine in cultured embryonic cells and observes loss of these regulatory marks with aberrant developmental gene expression. Which S-adenosylmethionine-dependent modification is most directly responsible for these two phenomena?

answers.A: Acetylation of lysine residues on histone tails
answers.B: Hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen
answers.C: Methylation of adenine residues in mitochondrial DNA
answers.D: Methylation of arginine residues within histones
answers.E: Methylation of cytosine residues within DNA

explanations.A: Histone acetylation uses acetyl-CoA rather than S-adenosylmethionine and does not establish imprints.
explanations.B: Prolyl hydroxylation requires ascorbate and vitamin C-dependent hydroxylases and has no role in gene imprinting.
explanations.C: Adenine methylation is a prokaryotic restriction-modification mark and is not the basis of mammalian imprinting.
explanations.D: Arginine methylation of histones modulates transcription but is not the heritable mark that establishes imprinting and X inactivation.
explanations.E: DNA methyltransferases use S-adenosylmethionine to methylate cytosine, the mark that underlies genomic imprinting, X-chromosome inactivation, and developmental gene silencing.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with higher-risk myelodysplastic syndrome begins a nucleoside analog that incorporates into nucleic acid and traps DNA methyltransferases, producing genome-wide hypomethylation. His oncologist notes that this class of drug increases neural tube closure defects in animal embryos and must be avoided in pregnancy. Which drug is he most likely receiving?

answers.A: Azacitidine
answers.B: Fomepizole
answers.C: Leucovorin
answers.D: Methotrexate
answers.E: Pyridoxine

explanations.A: Azacitidine and its deoxyribonucleoside counterpart decitabine inhibit DNA methyltransferases, cause DNA hypomethylation, are approved for myelodysplastic syndrome, and increase neural tube defects in animal models.
explanations.B: Fomepizole inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase and is used for toxic alcohol poisoning, not for myelodysplastic syndrome.
explanations.C: Leucovorin is a reduced folate used to rescue normal tissue from antifolates and to enhance formate clearance.
explanations.D: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and is a teratogen, but it does not act by trapping DNA methyltransferases.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine is the cofactor for cystathionine synthase and has no methyltransferase activity.

questions.question: A researcher reports that mouse embryos exposed to azacytidine have an increased incidence of neural tube closure defects, and that mice carrying DNA methyltransferase mutations show the same phenotype. A student asks how these findings inform the understanding of why periconceptional folic acid reduces neural tube defects in humans. Which interpretation is best supported?

answers.A: Folate prevents defects solely by supplying thymidine for DNA replication
answers.B: Lower SAM reduces DNA methyltransferase activity and may raise defect risk
answers.C: Neural tube defects arise only from mutations in folate transporter genes
answers.D: SAM has no role in DNA methyltransferase activity in the developing embryo
answers.E: Thymidylate synthase inhibition protects the embryo from these defects

explanations.A: Thymidylate supply is one plausible contributor, but these experiments implicate methylation independently of nucleotide synthesis.
explanations.B: Because carbon-loaded folate is needed to generate S-adenosylmethionine, the substrate for DNA methyltransferases, evidence that inhibiting or mutating those enzymes causes neural tube defects implicates reduced methylation capacity as one mechanism by which folate deficiency raises risk.
explanations.C: Most neural tube defects are multifactorial and are not explained by transporter mutations alone.
explanations.D: S-adenosylmethionine is the obligatory methyl donor for DNA methyltransferases, so this statement contradicts the biochemistry.
explanations.E: Blocking thymidylate synthase impairs DNA replication and would be expected to increase, not decrease, developmental defects.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a rare defect in S-adenosylmethionine-dependent protein lysine methylation is found to have low plasma levels of a compound normally generated when methylated proteins are degraded, and he has impaired long-chain fatty acid oxidation. Which compound is derived from trimethyllysine released during protein turnover?

answers.A: Adenosine
answers.B: Betaine
answers.C: Carnitine
answers.D: Choline
answers.E: Creatine

explanations.A: Adenosine is released when S-adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolyzed and has no relationship to lysine methylation.
explanations.B: Betaine is derived from choline oxidation and serves as an alternative methyl donor for homocysteine.
explanations.C: Protein lysine residues methylated by S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferases yield trimethyllysine on proteolysis, and trimethyllysine is the precursor of carnitine, which carries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria.
explanations.D: Choline arises from phosphatidylcholine and dietary intake rather than from methylated lysine.
explanations.E: Creatine is synthesized from arginine, glycine, and a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine, not from lysine.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease is found to have elevated plasma asymmetric dimethylarginine, a product released when methylated proteins are degraded. Her nephrologist explains that this residue is one of the two amino acid side chains most commonly methylated using S-adenosylmethionine. Which residue accumulates in mono- and dimethylated forms during signaling and transcriptional regulation?

answers.A: Arginine
answers.B: Aspartate
answers.C: Cysteine
answers.D: Glutamate
answers.E: Histidine

explanations.A: S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferases modify arginine to mono- and dimethylarginine, modifications used in signaling and in transcriptional regulation.
explanations.B: Aspartate is not a recognized target of protein methylation for epigenetic or signaling purposes.
explanations.C: Cysteine residues are modified by prenylation, palmitoylation, and disulfide formation rather than by methylation.
explanations.D: Glutamate side chains are modified by carboxylation in vitamin K-dependent proteins, not by SAM-dependent methylation.
explanations.E: Histidine methylation occurs rarely and is not the residue implicated alongside lysine in this regulatory chemistry.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for a suspected methylation disorder has cells that show abnormal cap structures and altered internal base modifications on messenger transcripts, with resulting defects in translational efficiency. Which macromolecular target of S-adenosylmethionine is most directly affected?

answers.A: Carbohydrate side chains on glycoproteins
answers.B: DNA cytosine residues in promoter regions
answers.C: Membrane phospholipid head groups
answers.D: Protein lysine residues in histone tails
answers.E: RNA bases and cap structures

explanations.A: Glycosylation uses activated sugar nucleotides rather than S-adenosylmethionine.
explanations.B: DNA cytosine methylation alters transcription and imprinting rather than transcript caps and translational efficiency.
explanations.C: Phospholipid methylation produces phosphatidylcholine and affects membranes, not transcript processing.
explanations.D: Histone lysine methylation regulates chromatin state rather than modifying the transcripts themselves.
explanations.E: S-adenosylmethionine is the methyl donor for RNA modifications including cap methylation and internal base methylation, which govern translation and transcript stability.

questions.question: A 26-year-old bodybuilder consumes very large quantities of a methionine-rich protein supplement. Studies show that his intracellular S-adenosylmethionine concentration is markedly elevated and his N5-methyltetrahydrofolate concentration is correspondingly low, with preserved total folate. Which regulatory relationship best explains this pattern?

answers.A: Adenosine directly inhibits methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.B: SAM inhibits MTHFR, decreasing formation of N5-methyl-THF
answers.C: SAM stimulates MTHFR, increasing formation of N5-methyl-THF
answers.D: Tetrahydrofolate inhibits cystathionine synthase when methionine is high
answers.E: Vitamin B6 inhibits methionine synthase when SAM is abundant

explanations.A: Adenosine is a product of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolysis and is not the physiologic regulator of this reductase.
explanations.B: S-adenosylmethionine exerts negative feedback on methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase, so when methyl group supply is abundant, less methylene-THF is committed to N5-methyl-THF and more remains available for thymidylate and purine synthesis.
explanations.C: Stimulation would raise rather than lower N5-methyl-THF and would create a futile cycle when methyl donors are already plentiful.
explanations.D: Cystathionine synthase is not the target of tetrahydrofolate inhibition, and high methionine actually favors transsulfuration.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine is the cofactor for cystathionine synthase and does not inhibit methionine synthase.

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl with a metabolic disorder is placed on a methionine-restricted formula. Within weeks she develops poor growth, hypoalbuminemia, and the plasma amino acid pattern shown. Her dietitian explains that methionine remains an essential amino acid despite the presence of an enzyme that regenerates it. Which statement best explains why remethylation cannot meet her needs?

answers.A: Betaine-dependent remethylation fully replaces all dietary methionine
answers.B: Homocysteine cannot be remethylated in the presence of cobalamin
answers.C: Methionine synthase only recycles homocysteine and adds no new carbon skeleton
answers.D: S-adenosylmethionine is produced from cysteine rather than from methionine
answers.E: Transsulfuration regenerates methionine from cystathionine and cysteine

explanations.A: Betaine provides an alternative methyl group but likewise only recycles existing homocysteine and cannot create new methionine carbon skeletons.
explanations.B: Cobalamin is required for methionine synthase, so its presence enables rather than blocks remethylation.
