explanations.C: Methionine synthase merely returns a methyl group to homocysteine already in the cycle, so it cannot create the carbon skeleton, and its capacity is insufficient to supply methionine for protein synthesis, which is why methionine is dietarily essential.
explanations.D: S-adenosylmethionine is made from methionine and ATP; cysteine is a product of the pathway, not a precursor.
explanations.E: Transsulfuration is irreversible in humans, so cysteine and cystathionine cannot be converted back to methionine.

questions.question: A 21-year-old student asks why the methyl group carried on N5-methyltetrahydrofolate cannot simply be transferred directly to DNA, phospholipids, and norepinephrine, avoiding the need for a separate cycle. Which explanation is most accurate?

answers.A: Cobalamin is required to activate the acceptor rather than the donor
answers.B: DNA methyltransferases are directly inhibited by tetrahydrofolate
answers.C: Methyl groups on folate are attached through a carbon-carbon bond
answers.D: SAM stores methyl groups so that folate can be recycled to purines
answers.E: The sulfonium ion of SAM makes its methyl group far more reactive

explanations.A: Cobalamin serves as the intermediate methyl carrier on methionine synthase and does not modify the acceptor molecules.
explanations.B: Tetrahydrofolate does not inhibit DNA methyltransferases; the issue is the chemical reactivity of the donor.
explanations.C: The folate methyl group is attached to nitrogen at position 5, not through a carbon-carbon bond.
explanations.D: Recycling folate is a consequence of the transfer rather than the reason a more reactive donor is required.
explanations.E: The methyl group on N5-methyltetrahydrofolate is not sufficiently reactive for most methyltransferases, whereas the positively charged sulfonium center of S-adenosylmethionine makes its methyl group a far better leaving group.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy with a complete block in the pathway that carries homocysteine out of the activated methyl group cycle is treated with a methionine-restricted diet. His metabolic physician adds a supplement of an amino acid that is normally produced by this pathway and which now becomes conditionally essential. Which amino acid must be supplemented?

answers.A: Alanine
answers.B: Arginine
answers.C: Asparagine
answers.D: Cysteine
answers.E: Glycine

explanations.A: Alanine is readily formed by transamination of pyruvate and does not depend on the transsulfuration pathway.
explanations.B: Arginine is supplied by the urea cycle and the diet and is unrelated to sulfur transfer.
explanations.C: Asparagine is synthesized from aspartate and glutamine and is not sulfur-containing.
explanations.D: The transsulfuration pathway converts homocysteine to cystathionine and then to cysteine, so a block in this route makes cysteine conditionally essential and requires dietary supplementation.
explanations.E: Glycine is generated abundantly from serine during folate carbon loading and is not limited by this block.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man undergoes isotopic tracer studies to quantify the fate of whole-body homocysteine on an ordinary mixed diet. The investigators measure the proportion that is remethylated back to methionine versus the proportion that leaves the cycle toward cystathionine. Which result is expected?

answers.A: About a tenth is remethylated and the remainder enters transsulfuration
answers.B: About half is remethylated and half enters the transsulfuration pathway
answers.C: Essentially all homocysteine is converted to cystathionine and cysteine
answers.D: Essentially all homocysteine is remethylated back to methionine
answers.E: None is remethylated unless dietary methionine is completely absent

explanations.A: This underestimates remethylation and would rapidly deplete the methionine pool.
explanations.B: On average about half of body homocysteine is remethylated to methionine and remains in the activated methyl group cycle, while the other half exits through cystathionine synthase into the transsulfuration pathway toward cysteine.
explanations.C: Complete transsulfuration would waste methionine and would defeat the purpose of the cobalamin-dependent salvage reaction.
explanations.D: Complete remethylation would leave no route for sulfur to reach cysteine and no way to dispose of excess homocysteine.
explanations.E: Remethylation operates continuously and is not conditional on the absence of dietary methionine.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman has followed a strict vegan diet for 7 years and takes no supplements. She reports tingling in her feet and difficulty concentrating. Her diet consists of lentils, broccoli, potatoes, fortified pasta, and citrus fruit. Her serum cobalamin is 110 pg/mL. Which food group would have supplied the vitamin she lacks?

answers.A: Beef, salmon, and cheese
answers.B: Broccoli, peas, and lentils
answers.C: Enriched breads and pasta
answers.D: Orange juice and other citrus
answers.E: Potatoes and dark leafy greens

explanations.A: Cobalamin is synthesized by bacteria and reaches humans through the meat and milk of ruminants and through fish and seafood, so beef, salmon, and cheese are rich sources.
explanations.B: Legumes and green vegetables are excellent folate sources but contain essentially no cobalamin.
explanations.C: Enriched grain products are fortified with folic acid rather than cobalamin, so they do not correct this deficiency.
explanations.D: Citrus fruits provide folate and vitamin C but no cobalamin.
explanations.E: Potatoes and leafy greens contain no measurable cobalamin.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man underwent ileal resection for Crohn disease and was told at that time that he would eventually need vitamin B12 replacement. He stopped his supplement immediately after surgery and remained asymptomatic for 4 years before developing paresthesias and a macrocytic anemia. Which statement best explains this long latency?

answers.A: Body cobalamin stores are about 20 mg and last only a few weeks
answers.B: Body cobalamin stores exceed 1.5 mg and last for several years
answers.C: Cobalamin is not stored at all and daily intake is mandatory
answers.D: Stores are held in red blood cells and turn over each month
answers.E: The daily requirement is 400 µg, so deficiency appears within days

explanations.A: A store of roughly 20 mg lasting weeks describes folate, whose deficiency appears far faster than cobalamin deficiency.
explanations.B: Normal body cobalamin stores exceed 1.5 mg, more than a hundred times the daily requirement of 2.4 µg, so reduced absorption may take years to become symptomatic.
explanations.C: Cobalamin is stored efficiently, which is exactly why the deficiency was delayed.
explanations.D: Red cells store most body folate, whereas cobalamin is stored predominantly in the liver.
explanations.E: The adult cobalamin requirement is only about 2.4 µg daily; 400 µg is the folate recommendation.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman underwent total gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Three years later she has a hemoglobin of 9.4 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 114 fL, and diminished vibratory sensation in the toes. Her terminal ileum is intact and her diet includes meat and dairy daily. Loss of which secreted protein best explains her deficiency?

answers.A: Cubam, from the ileal brush border
answers.B: Haptocorrin, from the salivary glands
answers.C: Intrinsic factor, from gastric parietal cells
answers.D: Pepsinogen, from gastric chief cells
answers.E: Transcobalamin II, from vascular endothelium

explanations.A: Cubam is a receptor on ileal enterocytes rather than a secreted protein, and her ileum is intact.
explanations.B: Haptocorrin binds cobalamin in the stomach but its loss is not the limiting defect after gastrectomy.
explanations.C: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells and is required for cobalamin to be endocytosed by cubam in the ileum, so gastrectomy abolishes physiologic cobalamin absorption.
explanations.D: Pepsinogen initiates protein digestion, and its loss does not by itself prevent cobalamin uptake.
explanations.E: Transcobalamin II carries cobalamin in plasma after absorption and is not a gastric secretion.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man with a rare autosomal recessive disorder has selective cobalamin malabsorption with proteinuria. He secretes normal intrinsic factor and has normal gastric acid, yet an oral dose of labeled cobalamin bound to intrinsic factor is not absorbed. Which step of physiologic cobalamin absorption is defective?

answers.A: Duodenal brush border transport by the proton-coupled folate transporter
answers.B: Gastric parietal cell secretion of intrinsic factor
answers.C: Hepatic uptake of cobalamin by transcobalamin receptors
answers.D: Ileal endocytosis of the complex via the cubam receptor
answers.E: Jejunal passive diffusion of free cobalamin

explanations.A: The proton-coupled folate transporter absorbs folate in the proximal small intestine and has no role in cobalamin uptake.
explanations.B: The vignette states that intrinsic factor secretion is normal, so the defect must lie downstream.
explanations.C: Hepatic uptake occurs after absorption and would not prevent a labeled oral dose from entering the body.
explanations.D: The cobalamin–intrinsic factor complex is endocytosed by the cubam receptor on ileal enterocytes, and loss of cubam function causes selective cobalamin malabsorption with proteinuria.
explanations.E: Passive diffusion accounts for only about 2% of a very large oral dose and is not the physiologic route being tested.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue and numbness in both feet. Endoscopy shows atrophic gastritis of the gastric body with loss of parietal cells. Serum cobalamin is 96 pg/mL, methylmalonic acid is elevated, and antibodies against intrinsic factor and parietal cells are present. She eats meat and takes no medications. Which diagnosis best explains her findings?

answers.A: Bariatric surgery-related cobalamin malabsorption
answers.B: Crohn disease involving the terminal ileum
answers.C: Dietary folate deficiency from inadequate intake
answers.D: Nitrous oxide-induced cobalamin depletion
answers.E: Pernicious anemia

explanations.A: She has had no gastric surgery, and her parietal cell loss is autoimmune rather than anatomic.
explanations.B: Ileal Crohn disease would impair cubam-mediated uptake but would not produce anti-parietal cell antibodies or atrophic body gastritis.
explanations.C: Folate deficiency does not elevate methylmalonic acid and would not explain the antibodies.
explanations.D: Nitrous oxide depletes cobalamin without producing autoantibodies or gastric atrophy.
explanations.E: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells with anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies defines pernicious anemia, which abolishes intrinsic factor and thus cobalamin absorption.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 3 years ago and lost 45 kg. She now reports numbness of both hands and a sore tongue. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 109 fL, serum cobalamin is 120 pg/mL, and methylmalonic acid is elevated. Her ileum was not resected. Which mechanism best explains her deficiency?

answers.A: Absent intrinsic factor after functional exclusion of parietal cells
answers.B: Bacterial overgrowth that consumes dietary folate in the jejunum
answers.C: Ileal cubam receptors destroyed by the surgical anastomosis
answers.D: Pancreatic enzyme deficiency preventing release from haptocorrin
answers.E: Reduced gastric acid preventing folate absorption in the duodenum

explanations.A: Gastric bypass functionally removes the parietal cell mass from the nutrient stream, so intrinsic factor is not available to bind dietary cobalamin, mimicking pernicious anemia.
explanations.B: Bacterial overgrowth can consume cobalamin but tends to increase rather than decrease folate, and folate is not the deficient vitamin here.
explanations.C: Her ileum and its cubam receptors were not resected, so the defect is proximal.
explanations.D: Pancreatic insufficiency can impair release of cobalamin from haptocorrin, but there is no evidence of it after this operation.
explanations.E: Folate absorption does not depend on gastric acid, and her elevated methylmalonic acid indicates cobalamin rather than folate deficiency.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has fever, diarrhea, and right lower quadrant pain that has recurred intermittently for 10 years. Pulse is 105/min. Examination shows 4/5 strength in all extremities and diminished vibratory sensation in the feet. Her studies are shown. Which additional finding is most likely on further workup?

answers.A: Dilated cardiomyopathy on echocardiography
answers.B: Elevated serum methylmalonic acid
answers.C: Increased hemoglobin A2 on electrophoresis
answers.D: Low serum homocysteine concentration
answers.E: Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test

explanations.A: Dilated cardiomyopathy is associated with thiamine deficiency, which does not cause macrocytosis or vibratory loss.
explanations.B: Chronic ileal inflammation from Crohn disease destroys the cubam-mediated uptake site, producing cobalamin deficiency with macrocytic anemia, posterior column signs, and an elevated methylmalonic acid.
explanations.C: An increased hemoglobin A2 indicates beta-thalassemia trait, which causes microcytosis rather than a mean corpuscular volume of 112 fL.
explanations.D: Homocysteine rises, not falls, in cobalamin deficiency because methionine synthase cannot consume it.
explanations.E: A positive Coombs test indicates autoimmune hemolysis, which would raise reticulocytes and bilirubin rather than cause posterior column signs.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 12 years has new numbness of both feet with absent ankle reflexes. His hemoglobin is 11.8 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 101 fL, serum cobalamin is 165 pg/mL, and methylmalonic acid is elevated. He eats meat daily, has had no gastrointestinal surgery, and has no autoantibodies. Which of his medications most likely contributed to this deficiency?

answers.A: Amlodipine
answers.B: Atorvastatin
answers.C: Metformin
answers.D: Sertraline
answers.E: Simvastatin

explanations.A: Amlodipine has no described effect on cobalamin absorption.
explanations.B: Statins do not interfere with intrinsic factor or ileal cobalamin uptake.
explanations.C: Metformin reduces cobalamin absorption, and long-term use is a recognized cause of deficiency that can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy.
explanations.D: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not impair cobalamin absorption.
explanations.E: Simvastatin, like other statins, causes myopathy rather than vitamin malabsorption.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for 3 weeks of progressive gait instability and numbness in his hands and feet. He inhales nitrous oxide from whipped cream chargers several times weekly. Examination shows absent vibration sense and a positive Romberg sign. Serum cobalamin is 310 pg/mL but methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both markedly elevated. Which mechanism best explains his findings?

answers.A: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells
answers.B: Dietary folate deficiency from poor oral intake
answers.C: Ileal disease preventing cubam-mediated uptake
answers.D: Irreversible oxidation of the cobalt atom in cobalamin
answers.E: Pancreatic insufficiency preventing haptocorrin release

explanations.A: Autoimmune gastritis lowers serum cobalamin, whereas his measured level is normal because the vitamin is present but inactivated.
explanations.B: Folate deficiency raises homocysteine but leaves methylmalonic acid normal.
explanations.C: Ileal malabsorption would reduce the serum cobalamin concentration rather than inactivate circulating vitamin.
explanations.D: Nitrous oxide oxidizes the cobalt center of cobalamin, inactivating the cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase despite a normal measured serum concentration, so both metabolites rise.
explanations.E: Pancreatic insufficiency impairs release of cobalamin from haptocorrin and would lower serum levels rather than inactivate the cofactor.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman with pernicious anemia has completed several months of parenteral cobalamin, her anemia has resolved, and her neuropathy has improved. She has severe needle phobia and reliably takes daily oral medications. Which regimen is most appropriate for maintenance?

answers.A: Cobalamin injections only, because oral therapy cannot work without intrinsic factor
answers.B: Cyanocobalamin 2.4 µg orally daily, matching the recommended daily allowance
answers.C: Folic acid 5 mg orally daily instead of cobalamin
answers.D: Intranasal cobalamin given only when symptoms recur
answers.E: Oral cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg daily

explanations.A: About 2% of a large oral dose is absorbed by a pathway independent of intrinsic factor and cubam, so oral therapy is effective when adherence is reliable.
explanations.B: A dose equal to the recommended daily allowance depends on intrinsic factor-mediated absorption, which she lacks.
explanations.C: Folate corrects the anemia but not the neurologic disease and can mask ongoing cobalamin deficiency.
explanations.D: Intermittent treatment triggered by symptoms allows demyelination to progress before it is recognized.
explanations.E: A daily 1,000 µg oral dose delivers enough cobalamin by intrinsic factor-independent absorption to maintain repletion in pernicious anemia.

questions.question: A healthy 68-year-old man asks his physician whether he needs any vitamin supplements. He eats a varied diet including meat and dairy, takes no medications, and has a normal complete blood count. His physician explains that a national body specifically recommends a change in how people of his age obtain one particular vitamin because of the age-related decline in release of the vitamin from food protein. Which recommendation applies?

answers.A: Adults over 50 should obtain cobalamin from a supplement or fortified food
answers.B: Cobalamin injections are required for all adults over the age of 50
answers.C: Increasing red meat intake reliably overcomes impaired release from food
answers.D: No supplementation is needed because tissue stores last a lifetime
answers.E: Routine folic acid supplementation prevents cobalamin deficiency

explanations.A: The Institute of Medicine recommends that people older than 50 obtain their cobalamin from a supplement or from fortified foods such as fortified cereals and soymilk, because crystalline cobalamin does not require release from food protein.
explanations.B: Injections are reserved for documented malabsorption or severe deficiency, not for all older adults.
explanations.C: Eating more meat does not overcome impaired liberation of protein-bound cobalamin in hypochlorhydric older adults.
explanations.D: Stores are large but finite, and absorption declines with age, so deficiency does develop in older adults.
explanations.E: Folic acid can correct the anemia of cobalamin deficiency while allowing neurologic injury to progress and does not supply cobalamin.

questions.question: A 6-month-old boy who has been exclusively breastfed is admitted in a coma. He developed normally until 4 months of age, then lost head control and became lethargic, irritable, and bruised easily. He is pale and flaccid and does not respond to painful stimuli. His mother is a strict vegetarian who takes no supplements. His studies are shown. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

answers.A: Congenital methylmalonic acidemia of the cblB type
answers.B: Dietary cobalamin deficiency acquired from the mother
answers.C: Hereditary folate malabsorption
answers.D: Iron deficiency anemia of exclusive breastfeeding
answers.E: Pernicious anemia with anti-intrinsic factor antibodies

explanations.A: Inherited cblB disease raises methylmalonic acid but does not lower the serum cobalamin concentration to 20 pg/mL.
explanations.B: An exclusively breastfed infant of a vegetarian mother with inadequate cobalamin receives almost none, producing severe deficiency with megaloblastic anemia, methylmalonic aciduria, homocystinuria, and neurologic regression.
explanations.C: Hereditary folate malabsorption causes megaloblastic anemia with low folate but normal cobalamin and normal methylmalonic acid.
explanations.D: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic hypochromic anemia without methylmalonic aciduria or coma.
explanations.E: Pernicious anemia is an adult autoimmune disorder and is exceedingly rare in infancy.

questions.question: A biochemistry student is asked to predict every metabolic consequence of complete cobalamin deficiency in a human. Her instructor tells her that, unlike bacteria which use cobalamin for more than fifty reactions, humans require it for only two enzymes. Which pair of enzymes is cobalamin-dependent in humans?

answers.A: Cystathionine synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase
answers.B: Methionine synthase and cystathionine synthase
answers.C: Methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
answers.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase and methionine synthase
answers.E: Thymidylate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase

explanations.A: Both transsulfuration enzymes use pyridoxal phosphate rather than cobalamin.
explanations.B: Cystathionine synthase is a pyridoxine-dependent enzyme and is unaffected by cobalamin status.
explanations.C: Methionine synthase requires methylcobalamin and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires 5'-deoxyadenosylcobalamin; these are the only two human cobalamin-dependent reactions.
explanations.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase is a flavoprotein and requires no cobalamin.
explanations.E: Thymidylate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase are folate-dependent enzymes with no cobalamin requirement.

questions.question: A 3-week-old girl has vomiting, lethargy, and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperammonemia after starting protein feeds. Urine organic acids show massive methylmalonic acid excretion with normal homocysteine. Her metabolic physician restricts the dietary precursors that funnel into the blocked cobalamin-dependent mutase reaction. Which group of substrates must be limited?

answers.A: Even-chain fatty acids and dietary glucose
answers.B: Glycine, serine, and threonine
answers.C: Leucine and lysine, which are purely ketogenic
answers.D: Odd-chain fatty acids, valine, isoleucine, methionine
answers.E: Phenylalanine and tyrosine, which enter as fumarate

explanations.A: Even-chain fatty acids yield only acetyl-CoA and never generate propionyl-CoA.
explanations.B: Glycine, serine, and threonine feed into the folate pool and pyruvate rather than into propionyl-CoA in a way that limits this block.
explanations.C: Leucine and lysine are ketogenic and bypass the methylmalonyl-CoA step entirely.
explanations.D: Propionyl-CoA arises from odd-chain fatty acids and from valine, isoleucine, and methionine, as well as from bacterial carbohydrate fermentation, and it is carboxylated and isomerized to methylmalonyl-CoA before the cobalamin-dependent mutase converts it to succinyl-CoA.
explanations.E: Phenylalanine and tyrosine are degraded to fumarate and acetoacetate without passing through propionyl-CoA.

questions.question: A 14-month-old boy has recurrent metabolic crises with markedly elevated methylmalonic acid that does not improve after high-dose parenteral cobalamin. He is exclusively formula fed with adequate cobalamin intake, and his neurologic examination shows hypotonia with white matter changes on imaging. Which laboratory pattern most strongly supports an intrinsic cblB defect rather than nutritional cobalamin deficiency?

answers.A: Elevated homocysteine together with elevated methylmalonic acid
answers.B: Elevated serum cobalamin with a low methylmalonic acid
answers.C: Low serum cobalamin with a normal methylmalonic acid
answers.D: Megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils
answers.E: Normal serum cobalamin with markedly elevated methylmalonic acid

explanations.A: Simultaneous elevation of both metabolites indicates that methionine synthase is also impaired, which is the pattern of true cobalamin deficiency rather than a selective adenosylcobalamin defect.
explanations.B: A low methylmalonic acid excludes the diagnosis entirely, since this disorder is defined by its accumulation.
explanations.C: A normal methylmalonic acid with low cobalamin would suggest an early or artifactual low vitamin level, not this disorder.
explanations.D: Megaloblastic anemia reflects impaired folate-dependent thymidylate synthesis and is a feature of nutritional deficiency, not of an isolated mutase cofactor defect.
explanations.E: A cblB defect prevents conversion of cobalamin to deoxyadenosylcobalamin, selectively disabling methylmalonyl-CoA mutase while methionine synthase and its methylcobalamin remain functional, so cobalamin and homocysteine are normal while methylmalonic acid is very high.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with untreated pernicious anemia has 8 months of progressive difficulty walking, worse in the dark. Examination shows a wide-based gait, a positive Romberg sign, and inability to identify a coin placed in his hand with his eyes closed. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T2 hyperintensity in the posterior columns of the cervical cord. Which combination of deficits reflects the affected tract?

answers.A: Absent vibration sense, impaired proprioception, and loss of stereognosis
answers.B: Hyperreflexia with spasticity and extensor plantar responses
answers.C: Loss of pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution
answers.D: Resting tremor with bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity
answers.E: Symmetric proximal weakness without any sensory involvement

explanations.A: The dorsal columns carry vibration, proprioception, and discriminative touch, so their demyelination in cobalamin deficiency produces loss of vibration sense, sensory ataxia worse without visual input, and impaired stereognosis.
explanations.B: Hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses reflect involvement of the lateral corticospinal tracts, the other component of subacute combined degeneration.
explanations.C: A cape-like loss of pain and temperature indicates central cord damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers, as in syringomyelia.
explanations.D: Parkinsonian signs arise from nigrostriatal dopamine loss and are unrelated to posterior column disease.
explanations.E: Pure proximal weakness without sensory findings suggests a myopathy rather than a posterior column lesion.

questions.question: A 55-year-old vegan man reports 4 months of tingling in both feet and unsteadiness. His complete blood count is entirely normal with a mean corpuscular volume of 88 fL and no hypersegmented neutrophils. His physician nonetheless orders serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid, both of which are abnormal. Which principle best justifies testing despite the normal blood count?

answers.A: Absence of anemia excludes a cobalamin-responsive disorder
answers.B: Neurologic symptoms often precede any hematologic abnormality
answers.C: Peripheral neuropathy appears only after megaloblastic anemia
answers.D: Serum folate must be low before neurologic signs can appear
answers.E: Vibration loss indicates folate rather than cobalamin deficiency

explanations.A: A normal hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume do not exclude cobalamin deficiency and can delay diagnosis until irreversible injury occurs.
explanations.B: In cobalamin deficiency the neurologic manifestations, driven largely by impaired methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and demyelination, generally precede the hematologic changes, so a normal complete blood count cannot rule out the diagnosis.
explanations.C: The temporal sequence is the reverse; neuropathy commonly appears before the marrow changes become apparent.
explanations.D: Folate status is unrelated to the appearance of the posterior column and lateral column signs of cobalamin deficiency.
explanations.E: Folate deficiency has only subtle central nervous system effects and does not cause vibratory loss or subacute combined degeneration.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and long-term proton pump inhibitor use has paresthesias and a mean corpuscular volume of 99 fL. Her serum cobalamin is borderline and does not settle the question. Her results are shown. Which test should be obtained next to confirm or exclude cobalamin deficiency?

answers.A: Anti-intrinsic factor antibody titer
answers.B: Complete blood count with peripheral smear
answers.C: Methylmalonic acid, serum
answers.D: Red blood cell folate concentration
answers.E: Schilling test with radiolabeled cobalamin

explanations.A: Antibody testing identifies the cause once deficiency is established but does not confirm whether she is deficient.
explanations.B: The blood count has already been obtained and is nondiagnostic in this borderline situation.
explanations.C: Serum or urine methylmalonic acid is the secondary and gold-standard test for cobalamin deficiency, because methylmalonyl-CoA mutase fails whenever functional cobalamin is inadequate even when the serum level is borderline.
explanations.D: Red cell folate assesses folate stores and cannot resolve an ambiguous cobalamin result.
explanations.E: The Schilling test localizes the site of malabsorption, is no longer routinely available, and again presupposes that deficiency has been confirmed.

questions.question: A 69-year-old woman with newly diagnosed pernicious anemia has a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 118 fL, a wide-based gait, and absent vibration sense to the knees. She is confused and lives alone with no assistance. Which initial therapy is most appropriate?

answers.A: Cyanocobalamin 2.4 µg orally each day
answers.B: Folic acid 1 mg orally each day alone
answers.C: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g intravenously once
answers.D: Injected cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg weekly at first
answers.E: Pyridoxine 100 mg orally each day

explanations.A: A dose equal to the recommended daily allowance requires intrinsic factor for absorption, which she lacks.
explanations.B: Folate alone can partially correct the anemia while allowing the neurologic disease to progress and is therefore dangerous in this setting.
explanations.C: A single 5 g dose of hydroxocobalamin is the antidote regimen for cyanide poisoning, not replacement therapy for pernicious anemia.
explanations.D: Parenteral cyanocobalamin 1,000 µg given weekly at the outset guarantees repletion in a patient with severe symptomatic deficiency, neurologic involvement, and uncertain adherence.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine supports cystathionine synthase and does not treat cobalamin deficiency.

questions.question: A 38-year-old firefighter is pulled from a burning building with soot around his mouth, a depressed level of consciousness, and hypotension. His oxygen saturation is 99% and lactate is 14 mmol/L with a normal carboxyhemoglobin. The toxicologist selects a cobalamin derivative whose cobalt center binds the offending anion so that it can be excreted in the urine. Which agent should be given?

answers.A: Cyanocobalamin, oral
answers.B: Deferoxamine, intravenous
answers.C: Fomepizole, intravenous
answers.D: Glucarpidase, intravenous
answers.E: Hydroxocobalamin, intravenous

explanations.A: Cyanocobalamin already carries cyanide on its cobalt atom and therefore cannot bind more; it is a supplement, not an antidote.
explanations.B: Deferoxamine chelates iron and has no affinity for cyanide.
explanations.C: Fomepizole blocks alcohol dehydrogenase and treats methanol or ethylene glycol ingestion.
explanations.D: Glucarpidase cleaves methotrexate and is used for antifolate toxicity.
explanations.E: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide on its cobalt center to form cyanocobalamin, which is renally excreted, making it the antidote for cyanide toxicity from smoke inhalation.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy develops a macrocytic anemia and oral ulcers. Her oncologist explains that the drug depletes the folate species that donates both a carbon and a pair of electrons in a single reaction of nucleotide synthesis, and that this reaction is the one most sensitive to folate depletion in dividing cells. Which reaction is impaired?

answers.A: Conversion of dUMP to dTMP
answers.B: Conversion of IMP to AMP
answers.C: Formation of PRPP from ribose 5-phosphate
answers.D: Reduction of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides
answers.E: Salvage of hypoxanthine to IMP

explanations.A: Thymidylate synthase uses N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate as both the carbon donor and the reductant to convert dUMP to dTMP, and this step limits DNA replication when folate is scarce.
explanations.B: Conversion of IMP to AMP uses aspartate and GTP and requires no folate cofactor.
explanations.C: PRPP synthetase uses ATP and ribose 5-phosphate and is folate-independent.
explanations.D: Ribonucleotide reductase uses thioredoxin-derived reducing equivalents rather than folate.
explanations.E: Hypoxanthine salvage by HGPRT uses PRPP and is unrelated to the folate pool.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with severe dietary folate deficiency is studied with isotopic tracers. Investigators note that although the largest quantitative use of carbon-loaded tetrahydrofolate in the body is purine ring assembly, the hematologic damage arises elsewhere. Which atoms of the purine ring are supplied by N10-formyltetrahydrofolate?

answers.A: Carbon 6 of the ring, which is derived from carbon dioxide
answers.B: Carbons 2 and 8, which are derived from N10-formyl-THF
answers.C: Carbons 4 and 5, which are derived from glycine
answers.D: Nitrogen 1 of the ring, which is derived from aspartate
answers.E: Nitrogens 3 and 9, which are derived from glutamine

explanations.A: Carbon 6 comes from carbon dioxide fixed onto the growing ring and requires no folate.
explanations.B: Carbons 2 and 8 of the purine ring are contributed by N10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, making purine biosynthesis the largest metabolic consumer of carbon-loaded folate.
explanations.C: Carbons 4 and 5 together with nitrogen 7 come from glycine, which is incorporated whole.
explanations.D: Nitrogen 1 is donated by aspartate in a folate-independent step.
explanations.E: Nitrogens 3 and 9 come from the amide of glutamine rather than from folate.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with severe folate deficiency has a hemoglobin of 8.1 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 116 fL, and 3 weeks of watery diarrhea. His cardiac, hepatic, renal, and muscle function are all normal. Which explanation best accounts for the specific tissues affected?

answers.A: Adipocytes require folate for triglyceride storage and lipolysis
answers.B: Cardiac myocytes depend on folate for contractile protein turnover
answers.C: Hematopoietic and intestinal epithelial cells divide most rapidly
answers.D: Hepatocytes carry out most one-carbon transfers in the whole body
answers.E: Renal tubular cells consume the largest share of cellular folate

explanations.A: Adipocytes are not rapidly dividing and are not dependent on folate for lipid handling.
explanations.B: Cardiac myocytes are terminally differentiated and do not replicate their DNA, so they are spared.
explanations.C: Thymidylate synthesis is required for DNA replication, so the fastest-dividing tissues, the marrow and the gastrointestinal epithelium, fail first, producing megaloblastic anemia and diarrhea.
explanations.D: Although the liver performs many one-carbon reactions, hepatocytes divide slowly and do not fail early in folate deficiency.
explanations.E: Renal tubular cells are not the largest folate consumers, and renal injury is not a feature of folate deficiency.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after cutting his hand at work. He lives alone, eats mostly bar snacks and fast food, and drinks four to six beers daily and twice that on weekends. He takes no medications. His laboratory studies are shown and the peripheral smear shows neutrophils with five or more nuclear lobes. Serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid are normal. Deficiency of which nutrient best explains his anemia?

answers.A: Folic acid
answers.B: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
answers.C: Iron
answers.D: Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
answers.E: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)

explanations.A: Heavy alcohol use with a poor diet depletes the small 20 mg folate store within weeks, and impaired thymidylate synthesis produces macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils while cobalamin and methylmalonic acid remain normal.
explanations.B: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes episodic hemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies, not macrocytosis with hypersegmentation.
explanations.C: Iron deficiency produces a microcytic hypochromic anemia, the opposite of a mean corpuscular volume of 108 fL.
explanations.D: Thiamine deficiency in alcohol use disorder causes Wernicke encephalopathy and high-output heart failure without megaloblastic changes.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine deficiency produces a sideroblastic microcytic anemia rather than megaloblastic changes.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with pernicious anemia has a hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 121 fL. Her red blood cell folate is low even though her dietary folate intake is unchanged and her gut is anatomically normal. Which mechanism best explains her low folate?

answers.A: Cobalamin deficiency directly inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
answers.B: Dietary folate is lost in the urine when cobalamin is low
answers.C: Excess SAM inhibits MTHFR and depletes N5-methyl-THF
answers.D: Homocysteine accumulates and blocks intestinal folate uptake
answers.E: N5-methyl-THF accumulates because methionine synthase cannot use it

explanations.A: Cobalamin has no effect on dihydrofolate reductase, which reduces oxidized folates independently of the vitamin.
explanations.B: Cobalamin status does not cause renal folate wasting.
explanations.C: S-adenosylmethionine is low rather than high in cobalamin deficiency, so its inhibition of MTHFR is lifted and even more folate is committed to the methyl form.
explanations.D: Homocysteine accumulation is a consequence of the block, not a cause of impaired folate absorption.
explanations.E: Without methylcobalamin, methionine synthase cannot unload N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, so folate is trapped in that form and becomes functionally unavailable for thymidylate and purine synthesis, producing a secondary folate deficiency.

questions.question: Two 68-year-old patients have identical degrees of cobalamin malabsorption after gastric surgery. One eats a diet rich in fortified grains and leafy vegetables and has a normal mean corpuscular volume with neuropathy alone; the other eats very little folate and has a mean corpuscular volume of 118 fL with pancytopenia. Which principle best explains the difference?

answers.A: A high folic acid intake makes secondary folate deficiency more likely
answers.B: Cobalamin deficiency always produces a secondary folate deficiency
answers.C: Secondary folate deficiency causes different problems than primary deficiency
answers.D: The lower the folic acid intake, the more likely secondary folate deficiency
answers.E: Vitamin B6 intake determines whether folate becomes trapped as N5-methyl-THF

explanations.A: A generous folate intake protects against the trapping effect, so the relationship is the reverse of that stated.
explanations.B: Cobalamin deficiency causes secondary folate deficiency only when folate intake is marginal; with plentiful folate the hematologic picture can remain normal.
explanations.C: Secondary folate deficiency produces exactly the same problems as primary deficiency, namely megaloblastic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and diarrhea.
explanations.D: Because cobalamin deficiency traps folate as N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, a person with a large dietary folate supply can still maintain enough usable folate, whereas someone with low intake rapidly develops functional folate deficiency.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine acts on cystathionine synthase and has no bearing on the methyl trap.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman being treated for anorexia nervosa has a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL, a mean corpuscular volume of 110 fL, and hypersegmented neutrophils. She has no neurologic findings and her gastrointestinal tract is anatomically normal. Which pattern of metabolite results would confirm an isolated primary folate deficiency rather than cobalamin deficiency?

answers.A: Elevated homocysteine and elevated methylmalonic acid
answers.B: Elevated homocysteine with a normal methylmalonic acid
answers.C: Low homocysteine with an elevated methylmalonic acid
answers.D: Normal homocysteine and a normal methylmalonic acid
answers.E: Normal homocysteine with an elevated methylmalonic acid

explanations.A: Elevation of both metabolites indicates cobalamin deficiency, since only cobalamin is required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase as well as methionine synthase.
explanations.B: Folate deficiency slows remethylation of homocysteine so homocysteine rises, but methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is folate-independent, so methylmalonic acid stays normal.
explanations.C: A low homocysteine is not seen in either deficiency, and an isolated methylmalonic acid elevation points to a mutase or adenosylcobalamin problem.
explanations.D: If both metabolites were normal, a clinically meaningful deficiency of either vitamin would be unlikely.
explanations.E: This pattern suggests a selective defect of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or its cofactor rather than folate deficiency.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with a mean corpuscular volume of 119 fL and mild gait unsteadiness is given 5 mg of folic acid daily before his cobalamin studies return. Six weeks later his hemoglobin has risen and his mean corpuscular volume has fallen to 92 fL, but he now has marked sensory ataxia and hyperreflexia. Which outcome does this course illustrate?

answers.A: Both the anemia and the neuropathy resolve with folate alone
answers.B: Hemolysis occurs as a consequence of folate excess
answers.C: The anemia improves while neurologic injury continues to progress
answers.D: The methylmalonic acid concentration normalizes with folate therapy
answers.E: The neuropathy improves earlier and faster than the anemia does

explanations.A: Folate cannot restore methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity or remyelination, so neurologic disease is not corrected.
explanations.B: Folic acid does not cause hemolysis, and his rising hemoglobin argues against it.
explanations.C: Supplying folate bypasses the trapped methyl folate pool and restores thymidylate synthesis, correcting the anemia, while untreated cobalamin deficiency allows demyelination of the dorsal and lateral columns to advance.
explanations.D: Methylmalonic acid remains elevated because folate has no role in the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction.
explanations.E: Neurologic recovery is slow or incomplete even with proper cobalamin therapy and never precedes hematologic response to folate.

questions.question: A 39-year-old woman with celiac disease has fatigue but a hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume at the lower and upper limits of normal, respectively. Her physician notes that folate is not included in routine chemistry panels and orders a metabolite that rises early when one-carbon transfer is impaired by either folate or cobalamin deficiency. Which serum metabolite is being measured?

answers.A: Bilirubin
answers.B: Ferritin
answers.C: Haptoglobin
answers.D: Homocysteine
answers.E: Methylmalonic acid

explanations.A: Bilirubin rises with hemolysis or ineffective erythropoiesis but is not a marker of one-carbon metabolism.
explanations.B: Ferritin reflects iron stores and acute phase activity rather than folate status.
explanations.C: Haptoglobin falls in intravascular hemolysis and is unrelated to folate or cobalamin.
explanations.D: Homocysteine is remethylated by methionine synthase using both folate and cobalamin, so it rises in primary folate deficiency and in cobalamin deficiency with or without secondary folate deficiency.
explanations.E: Methylmalonic acid rises only in cobalamin deficiency and would remain normal if folate alone were low.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a 30-year history of heavy alcohol use is referred for new-onset depression, poor concentration, and word-finding difficulty over 4 months. His complete blood count is normal, thyroid studies and head imaging are unremarkable, and serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid are normal. Which nutritional deficiency should be screened for next?

answers.A: Cobalamin
answers.B: Folate
answers.C: Niacin
answers.D: Thiamine
answers.E: Vitamin B6

explanations.A: Cobalamin has already been assessed with a normal level and a normal methylmalonic acid, effectively excluding functional cobalamin deficiency.
explanations.B: Depression correlates with folate deficiency, and screening for it is recommended in patients with new-onset depression, altered mental status, or cognitive complaints, particularly heavy alcohol users whose folate stores are small and rapidly depleted.
explanations.C: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra with dermatitis and diarrhea alongside dementia, which is not described here.
explanations.D: Thiamine deficiency presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion in an acute Wernicke syndrome rather than an isolated 4-month depression.
explanations.E: Pyridoxine deficiency causes a sideroblastic anemia and peripheral neuropathy rather than isolated depressive and cognitive symptoms.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman is brought in after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. For 5 years she has had visual and auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, memory loss, and disorientation, with slurred speech and progressive self-neglect. Head computed tomography is normal and seizures are controlled with carbamazepine, but her psychosis persists. Her studies are shown and antibodies against intrinsic factor and parietal cells are positive. Which management is most appropriate?

answers.A: Administer parenteral cobalamin along with her psychiatric medications
answers.B: Begin high-dose folic acid alone and reassess her in 3 months
answers.C: Increase the carbamazepine dose and continue observation only
answers.D: Prescribe pyridoxine with a low-methionine diet
answers.E: Start leucovorin infusions and discontinue all antipsychotics

explanations.A: Cobalamin deficiency from pernicious anemia can produce psychosis and a reversible dementia, and parenteral cobalamin combined with antipsychotic and antiseizure therapy is the treatment that resolves the psychiatric syndrome.
explanations.B: Folate alone would not correct her cobalamin deficiency and risks allowing further neurologic and psychiatric deterioration.
explanations.C: Her seizures are already controlled, and escalating carbamazepine does not address the underlying vitamin deficiency.
explanations.D: Pyridoxine and methionine restriction treat cystathionine synthase deficiency, which would raise rather than lower methionine and would not elevate methylmalonic acid.
explanations.E: Leucovorin supplies folate rather than cobalamin, and abruptly stopping antipsychotics in an actively psychotic patient is unsafe.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman whose first child was born with a lumbar myelomeningocele asks how to reduce the risk in a future pregnancy. She has regular menses, takes no medications, and eats fortified cereals occasionally. Which counseling is most appropriate?

answers.A: 400 µg of folic acid started at 12 weeks gestation is adequate
answers.B: Begin folic acid before conception because the tube closes by week 4
answers.C: Folic acid is unnecessary in women who eat fortified grain products
answers.D: Only women carrying MTHFR variants benefit from supplementation
answers.E: Supplementation should start after the first ultrasound is performed

explanations.A: By 12 weeks the neural tube has long since closed, so supplementation started then cannot prevent the defect.
explanations.B: Neural tube closure is complete around the fourth week after conception, often before pregnancy is recognized, so folic acid must be started before conception to support thymidylate synthesis and S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation during closure.
explanations.C: Fortification of enriched grains has reduced but not eliminated risk, and intake often falls short of the recommended 400 µg dietary folate equivalents.
explanations.D: Common MTHFR variants increase requirement, but supplementation lowers risk broadly and is recommended for all women capable of pregnancy.
explanations.E: The first ultrasound occurs well after closure, so this timing offers no preventive benefit.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with severe stabbing central chest pain. She has intellectual disability and no other known conditions. She is tall and thin with long digits, and slit-lamp examination shows the lenses displaced downward and inward. ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4. Deficiency of which enzyme best explains her presentation?

answers.A: Adenosine deaminase
answers.B: Alpha-galactosidase A
answers.C: Beta-glucocerebrosidase
answers.D: Cystathionine synthase
answers.E: Fibrillin-1

explanations.A: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency with recurrent infections rather than lens dislocation and thrombosis.
explanations.B: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, and renal failure.
explanations.C: Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease with hepatosplenomegaly and bone crises.
explanations.D: Cystathionine synthase deficiency causes classical homocystinuria, with downward and inward lens dislocation, a marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, and premature thromboembolism such as this coronary event in a young adult.
explanations.E: Fibrillin-1 deficiency causes Marfan syndrome, in which lenses dislocate upward and outward and intellect is normal.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with classical homocystinuria has healthy parents and one unaffected sister. His parents, who are second cousins, ask about the chance that a future pregnancy would be affected and whether their daughter could pass the condition to her own children. Which inheritance pattern applies to this disorder?

answers.A: Autosomal codominant inheritance
answers.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance
answers.C: Autosomal recessive inheritance
answers.D: Mitochondrial inheritance
answers.E: X-linked recessive inheritance

explanations.A: Codominance describes independent expression of two alleles, as in ABO blood groups, and does not apply to this enzyme deficiency.
explanations.B: Dominant inheritance would be expected to affect one of the parents, who are both healthy carriers.
explanations.C: Cystathionine synthase deficiency is autosomal recessive, so unaffected carrier parents face a 25% recurrence risk with each pregnancy and consanguinity increases the likelihood of homozygosity.
explanations.D: Mitochondrial inheritance would come exclusively from the mother and would affect all of her children to some degree.
explanations.E: X-linked recessive inheritance would essentially spare female relatives and would not be transmitted from father to son.

questions.question: A newborn nursery in the United States performs mandatory metabolic screening on every infant. The medical director explains that the panel is designed to detect pronounced cystathionine synthase deficiency, although it probably misses milder forms of the disease. Which analyte on the panel serves this purpose?

answers.A: Galactose 1-phosphate
answers.B: Homocysteine
answers.C: Immunoreactive trypsinogen
answers.D: Leucine
answers.E: Methionine

explanations.A: Galactose 1-phosphate accumulation identifies galactosemia and is unrelated to sulfur amino acid metabolism.
explanations.B: Total homocysteine is the metabolite that best reflects disease activity, but newborn programs screen for elevated methionine rather than homocysteine.
explanations.C: Immunoreactive trypsinogen is the screening analyte for cystic fibrosis.
explanations.D: Elevated leucine identifies maple syrup urine disease.
explanations.E: All United States newborn screening programs test for hypermethioninemia, which detects pronounced cystathionine synthase deficiency because homocysteine is remethylated to methionine when it cannot enter the transsulfuration pathway, though milder variants can escape detection.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl with newly diagnosed cystathionine synthase deficiency has a plasma homocysteine of 180 µmol/L. Her metabolic physician plans a therapeutic trial before committing to lifelong dietary restriction, based on the fact that some mutant forms of this enzyme have reduced affinity for their cofactor. Which initial step is most appropriate?

answers.A: A trial of high-dose pyridoxine, since some mutants respond
answers.B: Betaine alone, since it removes the need for any other therapy
answers.C: Cobalamin injections, since methionine synthase is deficient
answers.D: High-dose folic acid alone, which normalizes plasma methionine
answers.E: Liver transplantation as first-line therapy for all patients

explanations.A: Cystathionine synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate, and a subset of mutant enzymes regain meaningful activity with large supplemental doses of vitamin B6, so a pyridoxine trial is the standard first step.
explanations.B: Betaine is a useful adjunct that lowers homocysteine but does not replace cofactor trials, dietary management, or folate and cobalamin repletion.
explanations.C: Methionine synthase is not deficient in this disorder; cobalamin is given to ensure that remethylation is unhindered, not as primary therapy.
explanations.D: Folate is supplied to support remethylation but does not normalize methionine, which is already elevated in this disorder.
explanations.E: Liver transplantation can be curative but is far too invasive to be used before vitamin and dietary approaches are tried.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with pyridoxine-unresponsive homocystinuria has a plasma homocysteine of 150 µmol/L despite a low-methionine diet with folate and cobalamin supplementation. His physician adds an agent that lowers homocysteine by an entirely separate route that does not require folate or cobalamin. Which mechanism explains the benefit of this agent?

answers.A: Activates cystathionine synthase through pyridoxal phosphate
answers.B: Binds homocysteine directly and promotes its urinary excretion
answers.C: Chelates copper and reduces oxidative damage to the lens
answers.D: Inhibits methionine adenosyltransferase to conserve methionine
answers.E: Serves as a methyl donor that regenerates methionine from homocysteine

explanations.A: Cofactor activation is the mechanism of pyridoxine, which has already failed in this patient.
explanations.B: Betaine does not form a covalent adduct with homocysteine or increase its renal clearance.
explanations.C: Copper chelation is the treatment for Wilson disease and has no role here.
explanations.D: Blocking S-adenosylmethionine formation would impair every methylation reaction in the body and would not lower homocysteine.
explanations.E: Betaine donates a methyl group to homocysteine through betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, regenerating methionine independently of the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase reaction and thereby lowering plasma homocysteine.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl with cystathionine synthase deficiency is managed with a low-methionine diet, betaine, and vitamin supplementation. Her metabolic clinic must decide every 3 months whether her regimen is adequately protecting her from lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and thromboembolism. Which laboratory measurements best assess the effectiveness of treatment?

answers.A: Erythrocyte folate and serum ferritin
answers.B: Plasma ammonia and serum lactate
answers.C: Plasma homocysteine and plasma methionine
answers.D: Serum cobalamin and serum methylmalonic acid
answers.E: Urine organic acids and serum creatine kinase

explanations.A: Folate and ferritin monitor nutritional adequacy generally but do not reflect control of the sulfur amino acid block.
explanations.B: Ammonia and lactate track urea cycle and mitochondrial disorders rather than homocystinuria.
explanations.C: Plasma homocysteine reflects the accumulating toxic metabolite responsible for lens, skeletal, and thrombotic complications, and plasma methionine reflects both the dietary restriction and the degree of remethylation, so the two together gauge treatment effectiveness.
explanations.D: Cobalamin and methylmalonic acid confirm adequate cobalamin status but say nothing about the severity of the homocysteine elevation.
explanations.E: Urine organic acids and creatine kinase are used for organic acidemias and myopathies rather than for this disorder.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy has developmental delay, seizures, and marked homocystinuria. In contrast to classical homocystinuria, his plasma methionine is low rather than elevated. Serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid are normal, and cultured fibroblasts show accumulation of N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate. Which enzyme deficiency best explains this pattern?

answers.A: Cystathionine gamma-lyase
answers.B: Cystathionine synthase
answers.C: Methionine adenosyltransferase
answers.D: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
answers.E: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase

explanations.A: Cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency causes cystathionine to accumulate downstream of homocysteine and does not produce homocystinuria.
explanations.B: Cystathionine synthase deficiency raises homocysteine but also raises methionine, because homocysteine that cannot enter transsulfuration is remethylated.
explanations.C: Methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency causes isolated hypermethioninemia without homocystinuria.
explanations.D: Loss of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase prevents formation of N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, so homocysteine cannot be remethylated and accumulates while methionine falls, and the upstream methylene form accumulates with normal cobalamin and methylmalonic acid.
explanations.E: S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency blocks the production of homocysteine, so it causes accumulation of S-adenosylhomocysteine rather than homocystinuria.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man with untreated classical homocystinuria dies of a massive pulmonary embolism, and his plasma homocysteine had been persistently above 200 µmol/L. His younger brother's physician is asked whether the modestly elevated homocysteine found in many middle-aged adults carries the same implication. Which statement best reflects current understanding?

answers.A: Elevated homocysteine shows no association with cardiovascular events
answers.B: Homocysteine is a proven cause, and lowering it prevents infarction
answers.C: Lowering homocysteine with vitamins eliminates thrombotic risk entirely
answers.D: Thromboembolism in homocystinuria is unrelated to homocysteine levels
answers.E: Very high homocysteine correlates with thrombosis, but causality is unproven

explanations.A: Homocysteine is in fact strongly correlated with cardiovascular risk and mortality across populations.
explanations.B: Causality has not been established in the general population, and vitamin trials that lowered homocysteine did not reliably reduce events.
explanations.C: Vitamin therapy lowers the concentration but does not abolish thrombotic risk.
explanations.D: The extreme homocysteine elevations of untreated homocystinuria are closely tied to the thromboembolic deaths seen in young adults.
explanations.E: Elevated homocysteine correlates strongly with cardiovascular risk and, in animal models, accelerates atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, yet whether modest elevations are causative in the general population remains unclear.
